question: What are two advantages of using an Agile project management tool? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Consolidate project artifacts to a common repository.
optionB: Better relationships with business stakeholders.
optionC: Improve governance with gate steps in development.
optionD: Increased visibility into sprint and project status.
explanation:
Consolidating project artifacts to a common repository and increased visibility into sprint and project status are the two advantages, and both are about where information lives. An Agile tool consolidates the project's artefacts - stories, acceptance criteria, decisions, links to the change that implemented each one - into one place the whole team reads, instead of a scatter of documents and message threads. And it makes status continuously visible: the board shows what is in progress and what is blocked, and the sprint reports show whether the work will land, without anyone assembling a status update by hand.
The rejected options are outcomes rather than features of a tool.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Better relationships with business stakeholders) — a possible consequence of the visibility, not something any tool delivers by itself.
Option C (Improve governance with gate steps) — gate-based governance is a process the business chooses to impose; a tool can record the gates but does not supply the authority behind them.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-kanban
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: What are two roles a project Steering Committee plays in determining what methodologies are used? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Designing a methodology that will meet a particular project's requirements.
optionB: Approving deviations from the chosen methodology, when required to address project issues.
optionC: Enforcing that corporate project stage gates are part of the chosen methodology.
optionD: Setting the criteria for selecting Agile or Waterfall methodology to be used on internal projects.
explanation:
Approving deviations from the chosen methodology when a project needs one, and setting the criteria for selecting Agile or Waterfall on internal projects, are the two roles. A steering committee governs; it does not deliver. Both are decisions about policy rather than practice - the standard by which any given project is judged suitable for one methodology or the other, and then the exception to that standard when a particular project needs one. Both need authority above any single project.
Note that this item is governance practice rather than a Salesforce platform fact - no vendor documentation settles who sits on a steering committee. The references below describe the surrounding release governance and are orienting rather than decisive.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Designing a methodology for a project's requirements) — specialist work that a delivery or PMO function does, not a governing committee.
Option C (Enforcing corporate stage gates in the methodology) — an assurance activity carried out on each project, not a committee-level decision.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: At Universal Containers, Salesforce administrators are making changes to permission sets under instruction from the business. Randomly, various SOQL statements are failing. What strategy could be advised to bring this issue to the developer's attention earlier?
optionA: Ask administrators to only make changes to profiles instead.
optionB: Create a sandbox refresh strategy to ensure each sandbox is refreshed every day.
optionC: Extract each permission set, commit and merge to source control, and run through CI checks.
optionD: Advise developers to switch to SOSL queries that are more robust instead.
explanation:
Extracting each permission set, committing and merging it to source control, and running it through CI checks is the strategy. The failures are random because nobody can see the change that caused them. Permission sets are metadata, so the fix is to stop treating them as untracked admin clicks: retrieve them into the repository, commit them like any other change, and let continuous integration run the test suite against the result. Salesforce makes the same argument for the org development model - "a source repo can help to mitigate the pain point of keeping environments in sync. By externalizing the changes for each release, the team knows that the source repo reflects what they are delivering" - and a build that fails on the commit tells the developer which permission change broke which query, at the moment it happened.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Make changes to profiles instead) — profiles have the same invisibility problem as permission sets, so switching between them changes nothing.
Option B (Refresh each sandbox every day) — daily refreshes across every sandbox would destroy in-flight work to fix a visibility problem that source control solves, and most sandbox types cannot be refreshed daily anyway.
Option D (Switch to SOSL queries) — SOSL is a different search language, not a defence against a field the running user can no longer see.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has used Salesforce for the last 6 years with 50% custom code. UC has recently implemented continuous integration. UC wants to improve old test classes whenever new functionality invalidates tests. UC also wants to reduce the deployment time required. What should the architect recommend?
optionA: Do not execute any test classes in sandboxes and Production.
optionB: Execute all test classes in sandboxes and selected test classes in Production.
optionC: Do not execute test classes in sandboxes and all test classes in Production.
optionD: Test classes cannot be executed in sandboxes.
explanation:
Executing all test classes in sandboxes and selected test classes in Production is the recommendation, because the two goals pull in opposite directions and get different answers in different places. In the CI sandboxes, run everything: RunLocalTests executes "all tests in your org... except the ones that originate from installed managed and unlocked packages", which is what surfaces the old test classes that new functionality has invalidated - the stated goal of improving them. Time there costs nothing a user notices.
Production is where the clock matters, so narrow the set: RunSpecifiedTests means "only the tests that you specify in the runTests option are run", which trims the deployment window to the tests that cover what is being deployed. Note the granularity - runTests takes class names, one per entry, not individual methods.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (No test classes in sandboxes or Production) — a production deployment of Apex cannot skip tests, and running none in sandboxes abandons the goal of finding the invalidated tests.
Option C (No tests in sandboxes, all tests in Production) — inverts both goals: the invalidated tests are never found early, and running every test in production maximises the deployment time UC wants to reduce.
Option D (Test classes cannot be executed in sandboxes) — false; sandboxes run Apex tests exactly as production does.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers has five development teams. The performance of the teams has been good, but the number of bugs has been increasing. After each sprint, they need more time to understand the code and make changes. What are two ways to improve the performance? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Sprint review process.
optionB: Define a team that will analyze/approve all changes.
optionC: Define and follow code standards.
optionD: Version control system to identify who is generating the bugs.
explanation:
A sprint review process and defined, followed code standards are the two ways. The symptom names the cause: the teams need more time to understand the code after each sprint, which is a readability and consistency problem rather than a skill problem. Shared, enforced code standards are what make five teams' output legible to each other - naming, structure, error handling and trigger patterns that a reader can predict. The sprint review is the recurring point where the rising defect count becomes visible as a trend and the team can change how it works, rather than absorbing it sprint after sprint.
Note that this item is a team-process judgment rather than a platform fact - no Salesforce documentation settles it. The reference below is the closest official guidance on governance and change-management practice, and is orienting rather than decisive.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (A team that analyzes and approves all changes) — a central board converts a quality problem into a queue, and it removes the incentive for teams to own quality themselves.
Option D (Version control to identify who is generating the bugs) — attribution is available in any repository, but it does not reduce defects and it discourages the honest reporting that does.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is a global organization that maintains regional production instances of Salesforce. One region has created a new application to track shipping containers. The CIO has requested that this new application be used globally by all the Salesforce instances and further maintained and modified regionally by local administrators. Which two deployment tools will support the request? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Ant Migration Tool
optionB: Developer Console
optionC: VS Code with Salesforce Extension
optionD: Change Sets
explanation:
The Ant Migration Tool and VS Code with the Salesforce Extensions are the two deployment tools that support the request, because Metadata API tooling has no org-family boundary. Both authenticate to whichever org you point them at and deploy the same retrieved component set into each one, which is what shipping a single app to every regional production org requires.
Change sets cannot leave the family they belong to. They travel over a deployment connection, and "a deployment connection alone doesn't enable change sets to be sent between orgs" - each org must additionally be authorized to send and receive. Those connections exist between a production org and its own sandboxes, not between one region's production org and another's.
Currency note: Salesforce retired the Ant Migration Tool in Spring '24. It still runs, but receives no new functionality beyond API v59.0, and the Salesforce CLI is now the supported command-line route to the same Metadata API.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Developer Console) — edits one org in place and deploys nothing.
Option D (Change Sets) — confined to deployment connections between a production org and its own sandboxes, so they cannot carry the app across independent regional instances.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2024/01/moving-on-from-the-ant-migration-tool-to-sf-cli-v2

question: Universal Containers has just completed several projects, including new custom objects and custom fields. Administrators are having difficulty maintaining the application due to not knowing how objects and fields are being used. Which two options should an architect recommend? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create design standards to consistently use the description field on custom objects.
optionB: Create design standards with a document to store all custom objects and custom fields.
optionC: Create design standards to consistently use the description field on custom fields.
optionD: Create design standards to require help text on all custom fields and custom objects.
optionE: Create design standards to require all custom fields on all custom object page layouts.
explanation:
Design standards that consistently use the description field on custom objects and on custom fields are the two recommendations. The distinction that decides this is who each field is for. On a custom field, description is "description of the field" - documentation aimed at whoever maintains the org - while inlineHelpText "represents the content of field-level help", which renders next to the input for the end user. An admin trying to work out whether a field is still in use needs the first, and putting maintenance notes in the second shows them to every user filling in the form.
The practical advantage is that both descriptions are field metadata: they are retrieved, deployed and version-controlled with the component itself, so the documentation cannot drift away from what it documents.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (A document storing all custom objects and fields) — a separate register is accurate only until the next change nobody records, which is the situation the admins are already in.
Option D (Require help text on all fields and objects) — help text is for the end user filling in the form, not for the admin maintaining the org; maintenance notes there show to every user.
Option E (Require all custom fields on all page layouts) — a layout rule, not documentation, and it would clutter every page without telling anyone what a field is for.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: Universal Containers is adopting Scrum as an Agile methodology and wants to choose a software tool to support the adoption. What three key features of an Agile development support tool should an architect look for? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Work (for example, user stories or tasks) assignment.
optionB: Email notifications when work is created or changed.
optionC: Sprint backlog management.
optionD: Product backlog prioritization.
explanation:
Work assignment, sprint backlog management and product backlog prioritization are the three key features, because the question is specifically about supporting Scrum and those are what Scrum's artefacts require. A prioritized product backlog is the ordered list everything else is drawn from. A sprint backlog holds what the team has committed to for the current sprint, pulled from that product backlog. And work items have to be assignable, because a sprint is executed by named people picking up specific stories.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Email notifications on work changes) — a generic capability of nearly any tracker that says nothing about whether the tool supports Scrum.
Option E (Kanban board) — genuinely useful, but it belongs to Kanban, where "the workflow is mapped into columns" and work is pulled continuously rather than committed sprint by sprint; the odd one out by framework, not by quality.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-kanban

question: Universal Containers (UC) is considering implementing a minor change policy for a series of low-risk user stories that are commonly received by the UC admins. The policy would allow admins to make these changes directly in production. UC does not have continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) in place. Which three best practices should the architect suggest UC follow for their new change policy? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Downstream environments will not be automatically updated when production changes.
optionB: Minor changes do not need to be documented and can be made at any time.
optionC: Minor changes should be thoroughly documented and follow some type of standard cadence.
optionD: All changes should still be tested.
optionE: CI/CD is required to successfully manage minor changes.
explanation:
Downstream environments not being automatically updated, thorough documentation on a standard cadence, and testing every change are the three practices. A minor-change policy is a decision to accept some risk, not to abandon control, so the practices that matter are the ones that keep the change visible and reversible. Every change still gets tested, because low risk is an estimate rather than a guarantee. Every change is documented and made on a predictable cadence, so the org's current state can be reconstructed later and two admins do not edit the same thing on the same afternoon.
The third is the consequence nobody plans for: changes made directly in production do not flow backwards. Downstream sandboxes keep the state they were refreshed with, so the next release from a sandbox can overwrite a production-only change unless it has been reapplied there. Refreshing is what closes that gap, and a Full sandbox can only take that refresh every 29 days.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Minor changes need no documentation, any time) — the extreme that abandons control; undocumented production edits are exactly what the next release overwrites.
Option E (CI/CD is required for minor changes) — a change policy does not depend on a pipeline; the stem says UC has none and the practices above work without one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers requires that all sandboxes that have not been recently refreshed must also receive the newest changes to production. This must be done before any functionality from that environment can be moved to production. Which deployment tool would allow this deployment process to be managed in an automated fashion?
optionA: Change Sets
optionB: Workbench
optionC: Force.com Migration Tool (Ant)
optionD: Force.com IDE
explanation:
The Force.com Migration Tool (Ant) is the answer because it is the only listed option a machine can run. It is an Ant-based command-line client for the Metadata API, so a build server or scheduler can invoke it with no human present - which is what an unattended, repeatable step that must run before every outbound deployment requires.
Currency note: Salesforce retired the Ant Migration Tool in Spring '24. It continues to function but gains no functionality beyond API v59.0, and the Salesforce CLI is the supported command-line client for the same Metadata API today. The reasoning the question tests is unchanged - scriptable API tooling automates, declarative tooling does not - but a pipeline being built now should use the CLI.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Change Sets) — point-and-click by design; somebody has to build and deploy each one by hand.
Option B (Workbench) — an interactive browser tool with no scheduling or scripting surface.
Option D (Force.com IDE) — a developer's workstation environment that needs somebody clicking through it every time the sync is due.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2024/01/moving-on-from-the-ant-migration-tool-to-sf-cli-v2

question: Universal Containers has seven orgs in different regions. Its processes are global and standardized but each region needs the flexibility to be able to understand the global code and customize some aspects for its regions. Which development model is optimized for this need?
optionA: Create a centralized Git with all the code where the global team approves the changes made by the local teams.
optionB: Use unlocked packages to deploy the global code and allow each country to create its own customized unlocked package extensions.
optionC: Use a managed package for global code and another managed package for all regions' code.
optionD: Use a managed package to deploy the global code and allow local teams to request the addition of code within that package.
explanation:
Unlocked packages for the global code with per-country unlocked package extensions is the development model optimized for this need. It is the package-development pattern Salesforce designed for exactly this scenario: a base unlocked package carrying the global, standardized code and config, plus per-region 'extension' unlocked packages that depend on the base and add region-specific customization. Each region deploys base plus its own extension, can read and extend the base, and is in control of its extension's lifecycle.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Centralized Git with global approval of local changes) — a source-control workflow, not a development model for seven orgs; it puts every regional tweak through the global team and packages nothing.
Option C (A managed package for global code and another for all regions) — managed package source is hidden, so regions cannot understand the global code, and one shared regional package cannot hold seven different customizations.
Option D (A managed package with local teams requesting additions) — removes regional flexibility entirely; every change becomes a request to the global package owner.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/unlocked-packages-for-customers/break-up-your-metadata

question: Universal Containers is concerned that after each release, reports and dashboards seem to roll back to previous versions. Executives spend many hours crafting these dashboards to perfectly meet their needs, and are now questioning the Salesforce platform's ability to save things, even data records. What can the Salesforce architect advise to stop the rollbacks from happening?
optionA: Ensure report metadata is exported daily and that it is merged into the developer branches before the next release.
optionB: Use a third-party data warehouse.
optionC: Remove the executives' ability to change reports, and only allow developers to do that.
optionD: Back up all the reports just before the release, then reimport them after the release.
explanation:
Ensuring report metadata is exported daily and merged into the developer branches before the next release is the advice. Nothing is rolling back and no data is being lost - reports and dashboards are metadata, and a deployment overwrites the version in the target org with the version in the payload. The executives edit them in production; the pipeline still carries the older definitions that were captured when the branch was cut; the next release reinstates those. The platform is doing exactly what it was told.
The fix is to make the source reflect reality: retrieve the report and dashboard metadata from production regularly and merge it into the development branches, so the next release carries forward the executives' work rather than replacing it. That is the discipline the org development model is built on - "by externalizing the changes for each release, the team knows that the source repo reflects what they are delivering".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (A third-party data warehouse) — addresses reporting on data, not the loss of report definitions.
Option C (Remove the executives' ability to change reports) — removes the symptom by removing the capability the executives are paying for.
Option D (Back up reports before the release and reimport after) — the same merge done manually, once per release, with no protection against a second team editing in between.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: Universal Containers has recently acquired another business that uses Salesforce extensively. UC wants to merge their Salesforce orgs to effectively sell and service customers under one business. Traditionally, UC has followed an Agile development methodology to deliver Salesforce functionality. With the merging businesses, UC is convinced that adopting a Waterfall development methodology is the best approach. Which are two positive aspects of using a Waterfall development methodology? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Changes late in the process are expected and can be handled by integrating them into the requirements specs.
optionB: Milestones, timelines, and estimates tend to be more accurate and predictable due to the upfront due diligence.
optionC: The costs of starting the project are low since much of the design work is pushed to later stages of the process.
optionD: Complex processes that will need to be built are thoroughly understood and documented before coding begins.
explanation:
More accurate and predictable milestones, timelines and estimates from the upfront due diligence, and complex processes thoroughly understood and documented before coding begins, are the two positive aspects. Waterfall front-loads analysis, and its advantages are the ones that follow from having done that work before anything is built. Complex processes and their interactions are documented and agreed before coding starts, which is valuable exactly when the cost of discovering a dependency late is high. And because scope is settled early, milestones, timelines and estimates rest on something more solid than a guess, which is what makes the plan defensible to a business merging two operations.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Late changes are expected and folded into the requirements) — Agile's premise, not Waterfall's; the Agile Manifesto values "responding to change over following a plan", and Waterfall treats late change as rework against a signed baseline.
Option C (Low start-up costs because design is pushed later) — the reverse of Waterfall, whose design effort is the front of the project, not the back.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: When replacing an old legacy system with Salesforce, which two strategies should the plan consider to mitigate the risks associated with migrating data from the legacy system to Salesforce? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Migrate users in phases based on their functions, requiring parallel use of legacy system and Salesforce for a certain period of time.
optionB: Identify the data relevant to the new system, including dependencies, and develop a plan/scripts for verification of data integrity.
optionC: Use a full sandbox environment for all the systems involved, a full deployment plan with test data generation scripts, and full testing including integrations.
optionD: Use a full sandbox environment and perform test runs of data migration scripts/processes with real data from the legacy system.
explanation:
Identifying the relevant data with its dependencies and planning verification of data integrity, and performing test runs of the migration scripts in a full sandbox with real legacy data, are the two strategies - they attack the two ways a migration fails. Scoping the relevant data with its dependencies, and writing the verification scripts in advance, is what turns "the load finished" into "the load is correct" - parent records before children, external ids mapped, record counts and field-level checks proving integrity rather than assuming it. Rehearsing the whole migration in a Full sandbox with the real legacy extract is what exposes everything a design review cannot: the transformations that fail on genuine values, the records that violate validation rules nobody remembered, and the elapsed time of the load against the cutover window. A Full sandbox is the environment for that because it is "a replica of your production org, including all data" and is sized like production.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Migrate users in phases with parallel use of both systems) — a cutover strategy that manages the business risk of switching over, not the risk that the data arrives wrong.
Option C (Full sandbox with test data generation scripts) — rehearsing with generated test data hides precisely the defects a real extract would reveal.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Universal Containers is delivering many changes to its Salesforce system. Adoption reports are discovering that many features are unused. The steering committee wants this to change and is looking to the architect for advice. What should an architect recommend to overcome this?
optionA: Using Lightning Web Components for every user interface.
optionB: Sending weekly communication emails reporting on least engaged users.
optionC: Adopting user-centered design to understand user needs before building the solution.
optionD: Stop development until current features start being used.
explanation:
Adopting user-centered design to understand user needs before building the solution is the recommendation. Unused features are a discovery failure rather than a delivery failure - the team is building things correctly and building the wrong things. User-centred design moves the discovery upstream: watch how the work is actually done, prototype with the people who will use it, and test usability before committing the build. What ships then matches a need someone has, which is the only durable route to adoption.
Note that this is a design and adoption judgment rather than a platform fact; the references describe the surrounding lifecycle practice and are orienting rather than decisive.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Lightning Web Components for every interface) — a different UI framework changes how a feature is implemented, not whether anyone wanted it.
Option B (Weekly emails naming the least engaged users) — applies pressure to individuals for a product problem.
Option D (Stop development until current features are used) — leaves the same unused features in place and adds a delivery halt to the adoption problem.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: Universal Containers is in the final stages of building a new application to track custom containers. During a review of the application, a business subject matter expert mentioned that it would be nice to be able to track additional container types beyond what was originally scoped during the plan and design phase. Which two actions should be performed to mitigate the risk? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Have a discussion with the business SME and communicate that a new developer environment will be needed to mitigate the risk.
optionB: Have a discussion with the business SME and communicate that Salesforce has limitations in supporting such a feature to mitigate the risk.
optionC: Escalate and communicate to stakeholders the risk and mitigate it by allocating additional resources to support the new requirement based on stakeholder input.
optionD: Escalate and communicate to stakeholders the risk and mitigate it by extending the timeline of the project to support the new requirement based on stakeholder input.
explanation:
Escalating the risk to stakeholders and mitigating it by allocating additional resources, or by extending the timeline, are the two actions. New scope arriving late in the build is a risk to be surfaced, not a decision for the project team to take on the spot. Both keyed actions start the same way - escalate it to the stakeholders with an impact assessment - and then offer the two levers that can absorb it: more resources, or more time. Which one is pulled, or whether something else is dropped instead, is the stakeholders' call because they own the budget and the date.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Tell the SME a new developer environment is needed) — confuses provisioning with scope, and ends the conversation at the project team's level.
Option B (Tell the SME that Salesforce cannot support the feature) — not true, and asserting a platform limitation to avoid a scope conversation closes off a requirement the business may genuinely need.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is planning to release simple configuration changes and enhancements to their Sales Cloud. A technical architect recommends using change sets. Which two advantages would change sets provide in this scenario? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The ability to deploy a very large number of components easily.
optionB: A simple and declarative method for deployment.
optionC: An easy way to deploy related components.
optionD: The ability to track changes to components.
explanation:
A simple and declarative method for deployment, and an easy way to deploy related components, are the two advantages change sets provide here. For small declarative releases, change sets shine: they are point-and-click - no scripting, no command line - and the View/Add Dependencies button helps roll up related components into one set.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Deploy a very large number of components easily) — change sets are not good at large component counts; source-driven tooling is.
Option D (Track changes to components) — change sets keep no history or change tracking; that requires source control.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.changesets_inbound_deploy.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has development teams working on multiple projects. They are exploring a source control tool to track and manage their code/config. What two benefits does a source control tool provide? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Provides the ability for distributed teams to work in isolation.
optionB: Provides automated code/configuration deployments.
optionC: Provides the ability to automatically identify issues in code/configuration.
optionD: Provides the ability to back up code/configuration changes.
explanation:
The ability for distributed teams to work in isolation, and the ability to back up code and configuration changes, are source control's two core benefits. Feature branches let distributed teams work independently and merge their changes back together, and every commit is a recoverable snapshot, so all code and config history is backed up and reversible.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Automated code/configuration deployments) — a CI/CD capability layered on top of source control, not something the source control tool itself provides.
Option C (Automatically identify issues in code/configuration) — static analysis and code-quality tooling, again layered on top of the repository rather than part of it.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has two major releases every year and the team always runs into longer deployment times. In which two ways can UC reduce deployment time? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Specify the tests to run by using the RunSpecifiedTests test level.
optionB: Use recent deployment validations and the Quick Deploy feature.
optionC: Validate the deployment before migrating components to production.
optionD: Deploy components in groups to reduce deployment time.
explanation:
Specifying the tests to run with the RunSpecifiedTests test level, and using recent deployment validations with the Quick Deploy feature, are the two levers that actually shorten the deployment window. Choosing RunSpecifiedTests runs only the named tests instead of every test in the org, which is usually where the hours go on a large release. And a deployment that has already been validated against the target org can be promoted with quick deploy, which "takes less time than a standard deploy because it skips running Apex tests. These tests were previously run as part of the validation".
The eligibility window matters when you plan the release: the job ID returned by a validation "is valid for 10 days from when you started the validation". Validate early enough to be inside that window on deployment night and the production step becomes a promotion rather than a fresh test run.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Validate the deployment before migrating to production) — validating without then using quick deploy simply moves the same work earlier; the real deployment still runs everything again.
Option D (Deploy components in groups) — splitting the release adds ordering constraints and repeated overhead rather than removing any.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_quick.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation put the quick-deploy eligibility window at 4 days; Salesforce documents the validation job ID as valid for 10 days from when the validation started.

question: Which two statements are accurate about why Mock objects are needed when writing test classes? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: A Mock is needed whenever the code makes an HTTP callout.
optionB: Mock can also be used on the classes that extend the Batchable interface to bypass the batch jobs.
optionC: Some methods invoke long-running processes; using Mock is a shortcut for bypassing the long executions.
optionD: Using a Mock allows the test class to bypass the dependencies of other objects, methods, state, or behaviors. Therefore, the developer has total control over their own code.
explanation:
A Mock is needed whenever the code makes an HTTP callout, and using a Mock lets the test bypass the dependencies of other objects, methods, state or behaviors so the developer has total control over their own code. The first reason is a platform rule, not a preference: "by default, test methods don't support HTTP callouts, so tests that perform callouts fail", and the documented way through is to "enable HTTP callout testing by instructing Apex to generate mock responses in tests, using Test.setMock". Any code path that makes a callout therefore needs a mock before it can be tested at all.
The second is the general purpose of mocking: it replaces the dependencies a unit under test would otherwise reach - other classes, external services, unpredictable state - with responses the developer chooses, so the test asserts on the logic being tested rather than on whatever the dependency happened to return that day.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Mock Batchable classes to bypass the batch jobs) — not a real mechanism; Batchable is an interface a class implements, and the way to exercise batch code in a test is to run it between Test.startTest and Test.stopTest, not to mock it away.
Option C (Mock as a shortcut past long-running processes) — shortening a long-running process is a side effect of removing a dependency, not a reason mocks exist.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_interface_httpcalloutmock.htm

question: Universal Containers is looking to construct a continuous integration process to help manage code quality. Which three tools should be used to enable this? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Force.com Migration Tool (or SFDX CLI)
optionB: Continuous Integration build tool
optionC: Project management tool
optionD: Full sandbox environment
explanation:
The Force.com Migration Tool (or SFDX CLI), a continuous integration build tool and a source control tool are the three tools CI requires. Source control captures every change, a CI build tool (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps Pipelines and the like) runs the pipeline, and a deployment tool pushes the metadata into the target orgs and runs the tests.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Project management tool) — supports planning and tracking, but is not part of the CI pipeline.
Option D (Full sandbox environment) — useful for staging and performance work, but CI runs against scratch orgs or developer sandboxes and does not require a Full sandbox.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html

question: Which are two recommended methods of creating test data in Salesforce? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Utilize Heroku Connect to provide test class data.
optionB: Reference data from middleware directly within your test class.
optionC: Host a mock endpoint to produce sample information from an endpoint.
optionD: Load a CSV as a static resource and reference it in a test class.
explanation:
Hosting a mock endpoint to produce sample information, and loading a CSV as a static resource referenced from the test class, are the two recommended methods. Apex tests are isolated from org data by default, so the records a test needs have to be created by the test. Salesforce documents the static resource route for bulk data: store the records as "a comma-delimited file ending with a .csv extension" whose "first line of the file must contain the field names", then instantiate them in one line with Test.loadData, which "returns a list of sObjects that correspond to each record inserted". That keeps large fixtures out of the Apex and lets QA contribute rows.
For code that calls out, the data has to come from a mock instead, because "test methods don't support HTTP callouts, so tests that perform callouts fail" - an HttpCalloutMock implementation supplies the response the test needs, deterministically.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Heroku Connect for test class data) — makes the test depend on a data-sync service outside the org at run time: slow, non-deterministic, and a deployment failure when the external system is down.
Option B (Reference middleware data directly in the test) — the same dependency on an external system, with the same run-time and deployment failure modes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_load_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing.htm

question: Universal Containers' (UC) Customer Community is scheduled to go live in the EMEA region in 3 months. UC follows a typical centralized governance model. Two weeks ago, the project stakeholders informed the project team about recent changes in mandatory compliance requirements needed to go live. The project team analyzed the requirements and have estimated additional budget needs of 30% of the project cost for incorporating the compliance requirements. Which management team is empowered to approve this additional budget?
optionA: Change Control Board
optionB: Executive Steering Committee
optionC: Project Management Committee
optionD: Security Review Committee
explanation:
The Executive Steering Committee is empowered to approve the additional budget. The size of the request decides which body answers it. A 30% increase in project cost is a funding decision, and funding sits with the executive steering committee - the sponsors who own the budget and can weigh the extra spend against the consequence of missing a compliance deadline in three months.
Note that this division of authority is organizational governance rather than a documented Salesforce rule; the references orient rather than decide it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Change Control Board) — governs what enters the release and whether a change is approved for deployment, working inside the budget that has already been granted.
Option C (Project Management Committee) — runs delivery, plans, resources and schedules against that same envelope; it does not fund it.
Option D (Security Review Committee) — rules on security posture, which may define what the compliance requirements demand, but is not empowered to fund the work.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) just started configuration and customization of its Salesforce organization. The architect suggested the definition of an Application Lifecycle Management (ALM) process. What are three benefits of following an ALM process? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Training new users after each minor and major release.
optionB: Releasing new features on a consistent schedule.
optionC: Preventing existing working functionality from stopping.
optionD: Avoiding defects from being deployed to production.
optionE: Defining metrics for application development project success.
explanation:
Releasing new features on a consistent schedule, preventing existing working functionality from stopping, and avoiding defects being deployed to production are the three benefits. Salesforce frames application lifecycle management as five phases - plan, build, test, deploy, monitor - and says it "provides structure, guiding your changes from initial requirements through deployment and ongoing monitoring". The three keyed benefits are what that structure buys: a predictable release cadence instead of ad hoc pushes, protection for functionality that already works because every change is tested before promotion, and fewer defects reaching production because the pipeline gates them at each stage.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Training new users after each release) — change management, which a reliable release cadence makes possible but which ALM does not itself perform.
Option E (Defining metrics for project success) — a governance decision taken before the lifecycle starts, not a product of following it.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers has recently replaced a custom service center application with Salesforce Service Cloud. Administrators are now confused about which fields and classes are actively being utilized and how future implementations can be maintained. Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create an adoption plan for end users using Salesforce dashboards and reports.
optionB: Create a governance framework focused on high-level business strategy and goals.
optionC: Create a design standard requiring integration to use declarative configuration patterns.
optionD: Create a governance process requiring all projects to create project deliverable documentation.
optionE: Create a standard method for deprecating classes and fields using design standards.
explanation:
A governance process requiring all projects to create project deliverable documentation, and a standard method for deprecating classes and fields using design standards, are the two recommendations. The admins cannot tell what is in use, and both keyed answers create the record that would tell them. Requiring project deliverable documentation as a condition of delivery means each project leaves behind a statement of what it built and why, so the next person inherits intent rather than archaeology. A standard for deprecation handles the other half - the fields and classes that outlived their purpose - by defining how something is marked as going, communicated, and eventually removed, instead of being left in place forever because nobody is certain it is dead.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (An adoption plan with dashboards and reports) — measures usage by people, not by metadata; it does not tell an admin which fields and classes are live.
Option B (A governance framework for business strategy and goals) — operates above this question and records nothing about the org's components.
Option C (A design standard requiring declarative integration patterns) — constrains how things are built without recording what was built or why.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has two subsidiaries which operate independently. UC has made the decision to operate two separate Salesforce orgs, one for each subsidiary. However, certain functions and processes between the two orgs must be standardized. Which approach should UC take to develop customizations once and make them available in both orgs?
optionA: Develop the functionality in a sandbox and deploy it to both production orgs.
optionB: Create a managed (or unlocked) package in a Developer Edition org and deploy it to both production orgs.
optionC: Create change sets in a sandbox and deploy them to both production orgs.
optionD: Set up Salesforce-to-Salesforce to deploy the functionality from one org to the other.
explanation:
Creating a managed (or unlocked) package in a Developer Edition org and deploying it to both production orgs is the approach. A package is the mechanism designed for this shape: the standardized functions are versioned centrally, the same version is installed into each org, and later upgrades travel the same path - which is what keeps the two orgs standardized over time rather than only on day one.
Everything else on offer is confined to one org family.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Develop in a sandbox and deploy to both production orgs) — a sandbox deploys only to the production org it belongs to, so it cannot reach the second subsidiary's org.
Option C (Change sets from a sandbox to both production orgs) — a change set needs a deployment connection, which exists "between all orgs affiliated with a production org", so it cannot cross into an independent production org.
Option D (Salesforce-to-Salesforce) — a record-sharing feature that publishes and subscribes to data between orgs and moves no metadata at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers has many development teams deploying into a single org. The business is very seasonal and approaching its busiest season. The business owner asks the architect for advice about its next major production release. What best practice should an architect recommend?
optionA: Make declarative changes in production only.
optionB: Bypass regression testing for minor changes.
optionC: Developers should conduct user acceptance testing.
optionD: Avoid releasing near peak business periods.
explanation:
Avoiding releases near peak business periods is the best practice, and Salesforce's deployment guidance says this directly: release "at times when most users are off the system", "avoid peak hours when everyone's actively using the system", and steer clear of the period "right before holidays or major events". A seasonal business heading into its busiest weeks is that case exactly - the same defect that would be an inconvenience in a quiet month becomes lost revenue when every user and customer is transacting at once, and the team's capacity to respond is lowest precisely when the stakes are highest.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Declarative changes in production only) — removes the testing that a busy period makes more important, not less.
Option B (Bypass regression testing for minor changes) — assumes the minor label is reliable, at the moment a wrong guess costs the most.
Option C (Developers conduct user acceptance testing) — removes the independent business judgment that acceptance testing exists to provide.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000384452&language=en_US&type=1

question: What sandbox type would be appropriate for diagnosing reports of poor performance when accessing certain Visualforce pages?
optionA: Developer Sandbox
optionB: Developer Pro Sandbox
optionC: Full Sandbox
optionD: Partial Copy Sandbox
explanation:
A Full sandbox is the appropriate type. Sandbox Types and Templates names the Full sandbox as the one intended to be used as a testing environment that supports "performance testing, load testing, and staging", because it is "a replica of your production org, including all data, such as object records and attachments, and metadata". Reproducing a slow Visualforce page needs exactly that: view state, query plans and render times all track the data volume behind the page.
Note also that Salesforce does not permit performance or scale testing in production, so a Full sandbox is not merely the best environment for this work - it is the sanctioned one.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Developer Sandbox) — metadata only, 200 MB, no production data, so a volume-driven symptom cannot be reproduced.
Option B (Developer Pro Sandbox) — metadata only, 1 GB, again with no production data copied.
Option D (Partial Copy Sandbox) — carries only a sample defined by a sandbox template, capped at 10,000 records per selected object, so it cannot reproduce a volume-driven symptom either.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has a complex deployment coming up. The deployment will include several Apex classes which depend on custom settings that hold important configuration. How should an architect manage this deployment?
optionA: Manually deploy and populate the custom settings in production prior to the Apex class deployment.
optionB: Migrate the configuration to a Custom Metadata Type and include it in the deployment to production.
optionC: Manually deploy and populate custom settings in production using a change set.
optionD: Script the deployment of all functionality via the Force.com Migration Tool.
explanation:
Migrating the configuration to a Custom Metadata Type and including it in the deployment to production is how the architect should manage it. The split that decides this is metadata versus data. Custom metadata type records are metadata: the type and its records both move through change sets, packages and the Metadata API, so the configuration the Apex classes read arrives in the same deployment that delivers the classes. Custom setting records are ordinary data - the definition deploys, the values do not - which is why they have to be recreated in the target org by hand or by a separate load, in a second step that can be forgotten or done wrong. Moving the configuration to a custom metadata type makes the release self-contained and repeatable across every environment.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Manually populate custom settings before the Apex deployment) — keeps the two-step problem and only reorders it.
Option C (Populate custom settings in production using a change set) — a change set carries the custom setting definition, not its record values, so the data still has to be entered separately.
Option D (Script everything via the Force.com Migration Tool) — changes the tool without changing the fact that the setting values are still data the Metadata API does not carry.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custommetadatatypes_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_custommetadatatypes.htm

question: A Salesforce administrator has initiated a deployment using a change set. The deployment has taken more time than usual. What is the potential reason for this?
optionA: The change set performance is independent of included components.
optionB: The change set includes field type changes for some objects.
optionC: The change set includes new custom objects and custom fields.
optionD: The change set includes changes to permission sets and profiles.
explanation:
The change set including field type changes for some objects is the potential reason. A change of field type is not a metadata edit that lands instantly - it triggers a per-record data conversion. Salesforce warns that "the conversion runs in the background" and that "in some cases, the conversion can take over 24 hours to complete", with picklist-to-text and date/time-to-time among the slowest, and deployments also face a ceiling on the total number of field type conversions they can carry. On an org with real data volume that is by far the most likely reason a routine change set suddenly takes hours.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Performance is independent of the included components) — self-refuting; a change set's duration plainly depends on what is in it.
Option C (New custom objects and custom fields) — created empty, so there is nothing to convert.
Option D (Changes to permission sets and profiles) — rewrite access metadata, which is comparatively cheap.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.notes_on_changing_custom_field_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has multiple teams working on different projects. Multiple projects will be deployed to many production orgs. During code reviews, the architect finds inconsistently named variables and lack of best practices. What should an architect recommend to improve consistency?
optionA: Create a Center of Excellence for release management.
optionB: Use static code analysis to enforce coding standards.
optionC: Require pull requests to be reviewed by two developers before merging.
optionD: Execute regression testing before code can be committed.
explanation:
Using static code analysis to enforce coding standards is the recommendation. Inconsistency across many teams is a coverage problem, and only an automated check covers everything. Salesforce ships one for this: Code Analyzer "brings together different code-scanning engines, such as PMD, RetireJS, and ESLint, under a single, unified experience", runs from the CLI so it can be wired "into your build and deployment processes", and supports custom PMD rules for patterns specific to a team's own coding practices. Every commit from every team is then measured against the same rules, whoever wrote it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (A Center of Excellence for release management) — governs process rather than syntax.
Option C (Two-developer review on every pull request) — raises the cost of every change and still varies with whichever two people are reading.
Option D (Regression testing before commit) — proves behaviour, a different property; inconsistently named variables pass every test in the suite.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers is building a custom application on the Force.com platform. There is a budget and release date that has been set by the board of directors, but the application must meet the requirements that will be submitted and voted on by a public user community. What is the risk associated with the scenario?
optionA: The project is not using the Waterfall methodology.
optionB: The requirements should not be solicited by an external community.
optionC: The requirements are unknown and the release date has been set.
optionD: The project is not using an Agile methodology.
explanation:
The requirements being unknown while the release date has been set is the risk. Scope, time and cost cannot all be fixed at once, and here two of the three already are: the board has set the budget and the release date. The third is not merely flexible but unknown - the requirements will be decided later by a public community vote, so nobody can yet say what has been committed to. That is the risk, and it exists before any methodology is chosen.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Not using Waterfall) — a methodology choice is a response to this situation, not the risk within it, and no methodology creates capacity the fixed date and budget do not contain.
Option B (Requirements should not come from an external community) — unusual but legitimate; the problem is not where the requirements come from, it is that the commitments were made before they existed.
Option D (Not using Agile) — the same inversion of cause and effect as option A.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a customized repository that represents lots of different apps or projects. UC currently is trying to shift from the org development model to the package development model to manage changes. In the org development model, each developer starts their work within their own personal sandbox. When it comes to choosing development environments, what should a Salesforce architect recommend?
optionA: Start using scratch orgs that track all changes automatically and proceed with a staggered approach since scratch orgs can coexist with other models.
optionB: Start using scratch orgs because a developer can spin up a scratch org to start a new project, start a new feature branch, or start automated testing.
optionC: Keep developing in dev sandboxes, so that the developers feel no impact at all as they are used to sandbox development.
optionD: Keep developing in dev sandboxes because scratch orgs are not within the code deployment path.
explanation:
Starting to use scratch orgs because a developer can spin one up to start a new project, start a new feature branch or start automated testing is the recommendation. The Salesforce DX Developer Guide defines the scratch org as "a source-driven and disposable deployment of Salesforce code and metadata", and lists the moments to spin one up almost word for word as this option states them: start a new project, start a new feature branch, test a new feature, start automated testing, or start from a fresh org. That is the environment the package development model is built on - the org is described by the project's source and configuration files, so it can be recreated identically by any developer or by a CI job.
Sandboxes remain valid for org-development work, but a sandbox is a copy of an org rather than an expression of source, which is the coupling the package model exists to remove.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Scratch orgs track all changes automatically, staggered coexistence) — scratch orgs do not track changes by themselves; source tracking is a CLI feature against the project's source, and the reasoning offered is not the documented purpose of a scratch org.
Option C (Keep dev sandboxes so developers feel no impact) — keeps the copy-of-an-org coupling the package model exists to remove.
Option D (Keep dev sandboxes because scratch orgs are outside the deployment path) — false premise; scratch orgs are where package versions are built and tested before promotion.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers has written several validation rules and workflow rules for the Lead object. Which two test types should an architect suggest to ensure that a large inbound call center does not experience platform slowdowns under high call volume for the Lead object? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Unit Test
optionB: Performance Test
optionC: Load Test
optionD: Stress Test
explanation:
Performance testing and load testing are the two test types. The question is whether the org holds up under call-centre volume, which is what load testing measures - drive the expected concurrent volume at the Lead object and observe whether throughput and response times stay acceptable while every validation and workflow rule fires on each save. Performance testing is the companion measurement, timing the individual transaction so you can tell a slow rule apart from a saturated system.
Before any of this is scheduled, note the rules Salesforce places on it: "because Salesforce is a multitenant platform, performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox", and tests must be approved in advance - submit the request "at least one week before the testing date", since "unapproved testing is subject to throttling or blocking".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Unit Test) — answers whether the rules are correct, not how they behave under concurrency.
Option D (Stress Test) — deliberately pushes past the expected peak to find the breaking point, which is not the question the call centre is asking.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is starting a Center of Excellence (CoE). Which two user groups should an architect recommend to join the CoE? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Inside Sales Users
optionB: Call Center Agents
optionC: Executive Sponsors
optionD: Program Team
explanation:
Executive Sponsors and the Program Team are the two user groups to recommend. A centre of excellence needs the authority to decide and the capability to carry decisions out, which is what the two keyed groups supply. Executive sponsors bring the mandate, the funding and the ability to settle disputes between business units that no delivery team can settle. The programme team - architects, leads, project managers - is what turns those decisions into standards, reviews and a working pipeline. Salesforce's own org-strategy guidance describes the function in the same terms: a global centre of excellence should manage the business architecture and common standards across all of an enterprise's Salesforce instances.
Frontline groups are the people the CoE exists to serve, and their input belongs in requirements and design reviews; seating them on the governing body neither gives them what they need nor gives the CoE what it needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Inside Sales Users) — a frontline group whose input belongs in requirements and design reviews, not on the governing body.
Option B (Call Center Agents) — the same: end users the CoE serves, not the authority or capability it is made of.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question:
Universal Containers (UC) has recently acquired other companies that have their own Salesforce orgs. These companies have been merged as new UC business units. The CEO has requested an architect review the org strategy taking into consideration two main factors:
(1) The CEO wants business process standardization among all business units.
(2) Business process integration is not required as the different business units have different customers and expertise.
Which org strategy should the architect recommend in this scenario, and why?
optionA: Single-org strategy, as costs increase as the number of orgs go up.
optionB: Multi-org strategy, as it is uncommon for diversified business units to get used to working in the same space as other business units.
optionC: Single-org strategy, as the high level of business process standardization will be easier to implement in a single org.
optionD: Multi-org strategy, as they could deploy a common managed (or unlocked) package into the orgs of the different business units.
explanation:
A multi-org strategy, deploying a common managed or unlocked package into the orgs of the different business units, is the recommendation. Keep the business units in separate orgs and deploy a common managed or unlocked package into each one. That package is what carries the standardized processes: they are built once centrally and installed into every unit's org, so the processes stay identical without merging orgs that share no customers.
Salesforce's org-strategy guidance reaches this directly. The decision rests on the enterprise operating model, whose two axes are business process standardization and business process integration, and the CEO's two statements place this company in the Replication quadrant - standardization high, integration explicitly not required. For that quadrant the guidance is that companies "can (and probably should) have multiple orgs, however you should consider deploying a managed package from a central org into all of the replicated business units".
Consolidating into one org is the recommendation for the Unification and Coordination quadrants, where process integration is high. It is not high here: the business units have different customers and different expertise, so a merge buys the complexity of one org serving many lines of business and none of the shared-data benefit that would repay it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Single org because costs rise with org count) — cost is not the axis the operating model decides on, and the Replication quadrant explicitly tolerates multiple orgs.
Option B (Multi-org because units dislike sharing a space) — the right strategy for the wrong reason; the guidance rests on the standardization and integration axes, not on user comfort.
Option C (Single org because standardization is easier there) — consolidation is the Unification and Coordination answer, where integration is high; here integration is explicitly not required, and a package standardizes across orgs without a merge.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

corrected.note: Answer moved C to D. Salesforce's operating-model guidance maps high standardization with no integration requirement to the Replication quadrant, whose documented recommendation is multiple orgs plus a managed package deployed from a central org - not a single org.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is embarked on a large Salesforce transformation journey. UC's DevOps team raised a question about tracking Salesforce metadata throughout the development lifecycle across sandboxes all the way to production. As the deployment architect of the project, what should be the recommendation to track which version of each feature is in different environments?
optionA: Use an AppExchange or third-party tool that is specialized in Salesforce deployment.
optionB: Use change sets to track deployed customizations.
optionC: Use an Excel sheet to track deployment steps and document the SFDX commands.
optionD: Use Salesforce SFDX commands to deploy to different sandboxes.
explanation:
An AppExchange or third-party tool specialized in Salesforce deployment is the recommendation. The question is not how to move metadata but how to know where each feature currently sits. What the DevOps team is describing - an environment map, per-feature version state, deployment history and diffs between orgs - is the function of a purpose-built release management product layered over the same APIs.
Currency note: Salesforce now ships DevOps Center as a native option, and it appears alongside change sets and the Metadata API in Salesforce's own list of ways to deploy changes. It provides source-tracked work items and a pipeline view without a third-party licence, so an org choosing tooling today should evaluate it before the AppExchange products this item points to.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Change sets to track deployed customizations) — change sets deploy without recording a pipeline-level history of which feature version sits in which environment.
Option C (An Excel sheet of deployment steps and SFDX commands) — accurate only until the next deployment nobody logs.
Option D (SFDX commands to deploy to sandboxes) — the CLI moves metadata; it keeps no environment map or per-feature version state.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.deploy_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers' (UC) development team is using an Agile tool to track the status of build items, but only in terms of stages. UC is not able to track any effort estimates, log any hours worked, or keep track of remaining effort. For what reasons should UC consider using the Agile tool for effort tracking?
optionA: Allows the management team to manage the performance of bad developers who are slacking off.
optionB: Allows the developer to compare their effort estimates and actuals to better adjust their future estimates.
optionC: Allows the organization to track the developer's work hours for salary compensation purposes.
optionD: Allows the management team to make critical timeline commitments based solely on developer estimates.
explanation:
Allowing the developer to compare effort estimates and actuals to better adjust future estimates is the reason. Effort tracking earns its place by improving the team's own forecasting. Recording an estimate, then the actual, then the remaining effort gives the developer the feedback loop that makes the next estimate better, and gives the team a velocity stable enough to plan with. That is the inspect-and-adapt habit applied to estimation rather than to the product.
The three rejected reasons all repurpose estimates as a management instrument, and each one destroys the data that makes the practice work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Manage bad developers who are slacking off) — using estimates to police individuals teaches the team to pad every estimate.
Option C (Track work hours for salary compensation) — turns a planning tool into a timesheet.
Option D (Timeline commitments based solely on developer estimates) — treats a forecast with known variance as a promise, which is how a team ends up defending an estimate rather than reporting reality.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: The CTO at Universal Containers is complaining to the software development managers that he has no visibility of their teams' work status. What two software development methodologies should an architect suggest to solve this issue, and why? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: DevOps, because monitoring and logging practices help you stay informed of performance in real time.
optionB: Kanban, because one of its basic elements is to make everything visible, creating consistent transparency of work items.
optionC: Scrum, because openness is one of the five core Scrum values.
optionD: Waterfall, because it defines a fixed schedule and duration for each activity.
explanation:
Kanban, because one of its basic elements is to make everything visible, and Scrum, because openness is one of its core values, are the two methodologies. The complaint is about visibility of work status, and both frameworks are built on exactly that. Salesforce's own description of Kanban states it directly: "one of the basic elements of Kanban is to make everything visible, creating consistent transparency of work items" - work is written onto cards, the workflow is mapped into columns, and the position of every card shows its state at a glance, so "it's easy for teams to know when delays occur". Scrum reaches the same place through its ceremonies and values: teams are expected to be transparent about progress and to speak up when assumptions turn out wrong, and the inspect-and-adapt cadence puts that in front of everyone on a fixed rhythm.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (DevOps monitoring and logging) — reports on how the deployed system is performing, a different subject from where the teams' work has got to.
Option D (Waterfall's fixed schedule) — publishes a plan rather than a status; it says what should be happening this week, not what is.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-kanban
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum

question: Universal Containers (UC) is planning for a huge data migration as part of their Service Cloud implementation. UC has approximately 15 million customers, 30 million contacts, and 30 million active cases. Which two key areas of UC's data migration test plan should be included? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Target Salesforce server and source system IP addresses.
optionB: Manual and automated data validation approaches.
optionC: Success criteria for data migration.
optionD: APIs to be used for data migration.
explanation:
Manual and automated data validation approaches, and success criteria for the data migration, are the two key areas of the test plan.
