A test plan needs explicit success criteria - what good looks like: record counts match, key fields populated, integrity checks pass, throughput within the window - and the validation methods that will be used to test against those criteria: automated count, checksum and field-level checks plus manual spot-checks.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Target server and source system IP addresses) — infrastructure detail, not test-plan content.
Option D (APIs to be used for the migration) — a design decision about how the load runs, not how it is tested.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to introduce data volume testing to resolve ongoing performance defects earlier in the lifecycle. Regulations prohibit the use of production data in non-production environments. Which two options can the architect recommend? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use Query Analyzer in production.
optionB: Request a partial sandbox copy after the next Salesforce release.
optionC: Generate mock data that mimics production data shape and volume.
optionD: Perform data masking on a Full sandbox after a refresh.
explanation:
Generating mock data that mimics production shape and volume, and performing data masking on a Full sandbox after a refresh, are the two options - both reach production-like volume without moving regulated data downstream. Salesforce Data Mask runs "in full or partial sandboxes" and is installed as a managed package in production, with the masking job executing only in the sandbox so production is never touched; the result cannot be unmasked, which is what makes a masked Full sandbox safe to hand to a testing team. Generating synthetic data that mirrors production's row counts and distribution reaches the same volumes with no real records involved at all.
Currency note: the article is now titled "Secure Your Sandbox Data with Salesforce Data Mask (Legacy)". The managed package reaches end of service on 31 December 2026 and Salesforce directs customers to Data Mask & Seed. The masking approach is unchanged; the product name is not.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Query Analyzer in production) — inspects query plans; it provides no environment to test in.
Option B (A Partial Copy after the next release) — still copies real production records, so it does not satisfy the regulation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_mask_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is considering updating their Salesforce production deployment as a part of their release management process. Which three best practices should UC consider for production deployment? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Define a rollback strategy.
optionB: Announce the maintenance window ahead of time.
optionC: Alert all users on the day of deployment.
optionD: Temporarily suspend configuration changes in production.
explanation:
Defining a rollback strategy, announcing the maintenance window ahead of time, and temporarily suspending configuration changes in production are the three best practices - they cover the three things that go wrong on deployment night. A rollback strategy has to be designed in advance, because reversing a release is not a single command - restoring changed components means redeploying the previous state, and removing new ones means a destructiveChanges manifest naming them. Announcing the maintenance window ahead of time lets users plan around it, which is also the point of Salesforce's advice to release when most users are off the system. And freezing configuration changes in production during the window keeps an administrator's edit from colliding with the release - the platform enforces part of this itself, since a deployment takes an org lock that blocks setup changes until it completes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Alert all users on the day of deployment) — the same communication, too late to be acted on.
Option E (Schedule releases with Salesforce upgrades) — stacks two sources of change on one weekend, which makes any resulting defect harder to attribute, not easier.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy_deleting_files.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000384452&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a high-tech company using SFDX tools and methodologies for its Salesforce development. UC has moved some of its code and configuration to unlocked packages. Which two best practices should an architect recommend to support UC's new package development strategy? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Test developed packages in test environments before installing to production.
optionB: Move everything in the existing codebase to a single monolithic package.
optionC: Consult the Metadata Coverage report to identify features supported by packages.
optionD: Version control does not need to be used, as packages manage all the code and configuration.
explanation:
Testing developed packages in test environments before installing to production, and consulting the Metadata Coverage report to identify features supported by packages, are the two best practices that keep a package strategy honest. Install each package version into a scratch org or sandbox before it reaches production - installation exercises dependencies, namespace resolution and version ordering, none of which the build step proves. And check the Metadata Coverage Report, which lists every metadata type against the channels that can carry it, including Metadata API, change sets, unlocked packaging, managed packaging and source tracking; it is how you find out that a component you intended to package cannot be packaged before the split is designed around it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Move everything to a single monolithic package) — restores the single tangled unit that packaging exists to break up.
Option D (Version control is unnecessary with packages) — inverted; version control is more important under package development, not less, because the package version is built from source and the repository is the record of what a version contains.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/metadata-coverage
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has been following the Waterfall methodology to deliver customer apps in Salesforce. As the business is growing at scale and with demand to incorporate features and functionality at faster pace, UC is finding the Waterfall approach is not optimal, and intends to transition towards an Agile development methodology. Which are two strengths of using an Agile development methodology? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Careful documentation is done at each step of the process so a target body of knowledge is available for inspection.
optionB: The project requirements in later phases are expected and accommodated by the process, by design.
optionC: All elements of the build are fully understood before work begins, reducing risk of unpleasant surprises.
optionD: There are many small releases of functional code, allowing stakeholders to see and touch the work in progress.
explanation:
Later-phase requirements being expected and accommodated by design, and many small releases of functional code that stakeholders can see and touch, are Agile's two strengths here - the ones the Agile Manifesto states as values. Requirements that arrive later are handled by design rather than treated as a breach of the plan - "responding to change over following a plan" - which is what a business growing at scale needs when next quarter's requirement is not yet known. And the work is delivered in many small increments, so stakeholders see and use working functionality early instead of waiting for a single delivery at the end: "working software over comprehensive documentation".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Careful documentation at each step for inspection) — a strength of the "document-heavy, design-it-all-up-front process" the Agile signatories were reacting against.
Option C (Everything fully understood before work begins) — the Waterfall premise, identified by the Manifesto's authors as the source of large, expensive, often-aborted projects.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: Ursa Major Solar (UMS) has used Aura components significantly in its Salesforce application development. UMS has established a robust test framework and the development team follows Salesforce-recommended testing practices. The UMS team uses Salesforce's test tool to check for common accessibility issues. In which two environments can the UMS team call Aura accessibility tests? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: WebDriver Test
optionB: JS Test (Jasmine)
optionC: AuraDriver Test
optionD: ACCTEST
explanation:
WebDriver tests and JS tests (Jasmine) are the two environments. Salesforce answers this in one sentence: "You can call Aura accessibility tests in two environments. For JavaScript tests, use $A.test.assertAccessible(). For WebDriver tests, use auraTestingUtil.assertAccessible()." Both evaluate the rendered DOM against Salesforce's accessibility rules and return an empty string on success or the failing rules on failure, so the same checks run whether the component is exercised from a JavaScript test or driven through a browser. Naming the method that belongs to each environment is what the question is really testing, since calling the JavaScript form from a WebDriver test does not work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (AuraDriver Test) — not an environment the framework provides; there is no AuraDriver test type.
Option D (ACCTEST) — likewise invented; no ACCTEST harness exists.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/accessibility_write_tests.htm

question: Cloud Kicks (CK) is launching a new sneaker line during the upcoming holiday season and needs to do thorough batch data testing before go-live. CK is using Salesforce Unlimited Edition. What two sandbox types should the architect recommend for batch data testing? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Developer Sandbox
optionB: Partial Copy Sandbox
optionC: Developer Pro Sandbox
optionD: Full Sandbox
explanation:
A Partial Copy sandbox and a Full sandbox are the two types to recommend, because batch testing requires real data volumes and only those two carry production data - Partial via a sandbox template with up to 5 GB, Full as a complete replica of production.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Developer Sandbox) — 200 MB of metadata only, with no production data, so it cannot realistically test batch jobs.
Option C (Developer Pro Sandbox) — 1 GB, still metadata only, with the same limitation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has four different business units (BUs) with different processes that share global customers. They have implemented a multi-org strategy with one org consolidating customer 360-degree view, and four orgs for the different BUs. Each of the BU orgs reads and writes customer information from/to the customer 360-degree view org in real time. UC is now launching a new BU that will use Salesforce. It does not share customers with the other BUs and needs flexibility in their business processes. What should an architect recommend as org strategy for this new BU?
optionA: Use the same Salesforce org of another BU that shares geographical localization with the new BU.
optionB: Use a new Salesforce org for the new BU, and customize integration so that it reads and writes customer information from the customer data org.
optionC: Use a new stand-alone Salesforce org for the new BU, not integrated with the others.
optionD: Deploy the new BU in the customer 360-degree view org, and read/write customer information from it without need of custom integration.
explanation:
A new stand-alone Salesforce org for the new BU, not integrated with the others, is the recommendation. On the operating-model framework Salesforce uses for org strategy, this new business unit is low on both axes: it shares no customers with the others, so there is no process integration to preserve, and it needs its own processes, so there is no standardization to enforce. That is the Diversification quadrant, where the guidance is that such companies "will probably always have multiple orgs" because the work to consolidate different business processes and data models into one org "is usually very complicated". A stand-alone org therefore gives the new unit full autonomy at no cost to anyone else.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Share another BU's org by geography) — imposes that unit's processes on a business chosen for its flexibility.
Option B (New org integrated with the customer data org) — buys integration for records that do not overlap with any other unit's.
Option D (Deploy inside the customer 360 org) — puts a unit with no shared customers into the shared-customer hub, adding its distinct processes to the org whose job is consolidation.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers (UC) works with different partners and has few admin resources that take care of the day-to-day deployment tasks. As a result, UC would like to find a way to automate the deployments using Metadata API. Which two limitations of Metadata API should be considered when using Metadata API-based deployments? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Deploy and retrieve up to 10,000 files at once.
optionB: Maximum size of deployed .zip file is 400 MB.
optionC: Maximum size of deployed .zip file is 39 MB.
optionD: Deploy up to 10,000 files, but retrieve more than 10,000 files.
explanation:
Deploying and retrieving up to 10,000 files at once, and a 39 MB maximum for the deployed .zip file, are the two limitations. Salesforce documents both in the same place: "You can deploy or retrieve up to 10,000 files at once", and "the maximum size of the deployed or retrieved .zip file is 39 MB". Base-64 encoding inflates the payload, so the compressed archive has to stay under roughly that figure before encoding to fit inside the SOAP message limit.
One figure to have right: the companion limit on the uncompressed contents is "600 MB or 629,145,600 bytes", not 400 MB. Both constraints apply at once - a package can fail the uncompressed ceiling while its .zip is comfortably under 39 MB.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Maximum .zip size 400 MB) — not the archive limit under any reading; the .zip cap is 39 MB and even the uncompressed ceiling is 600 MB.
Option D (Deploy 10,000 but retrieve more) — the file cap applies symmetrically to deploy and retrieve.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet.meta/salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet/salesforce_app_limits_platform_metadata.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation taught the uncompressed limit as 400 MB; Salesforce documents it as 600 MB (629,145,600 bytes). The 39 MB .zip figure it gave is correct.

question: What are two limitations an architect should consider when designing a strategy for managing technical reference data with multiple related objects? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Apex CPU limits
optionB: Circular relationships
optionC: HTTP response size
optionD: Depth of nested relationships
explanation:
Circular relationships and the depth of nested relationships are the two limitations, and both are design-time constraints on the shape of the reference data itself. Relationship queries cannot traverse indefinitely: "in each specified relationship, no more than five levels can be specified in a child-to-parent relationship", and there are ceilings on breadth too - no more than 55 child-to-parent relationships and no more than 20 parent-to-child relationships in a single query. A reference model nested more deeply than that cannot be read in one query no matter how the code is written. Circular relationship chains are the other structural trap: a cycle among related reference objects cannot be loaded or traversed in a defined order.
One version detail worth carrying: the parent-to-child depth moved. It is up to five levels in API version 58.0 and later, but only two levels in 57.0 and earlier, so a query that works today can fail against an older manifest version.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex CPU limits) — a real limit, but it binds at run time on a particular transaction rather than constraining how the reference data may be modelled.
Option C (HTTP response size) — likewise a run-time transport limit, not a data-model constraint.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.soql_sosl.meta/soql_sosl/sforce_api_calls_soql_relationships_query_limits.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) recently acquired Eastern Trail Outfitters (ETO). NTO's sales leadership team had hands-on experience with ETO's Sales Optimization app and have given the feedback that the app would benefit NTO's sales team. Which option should the architect recommend for having ETO's Sales Optimization app in NTO's Salesforce org in the shortest possible time?
optionA: Create an unmanaged package of the app and deploy in NTO's org.
optionB: Create users in ETO's org and provide access to NTO's sales team.
optionC: Create a core team and build the Sales Optimization app in NTO's org.
optionD: Create a managed package of the app and deploy in NTO's org.
explanation:
Creating an unmanaged package of the app and deploying it in NTO's org is the recommendation. The question sets one criterion - shortest possible time - and an unmanaged package is the mechanism Salesforce documents for exactly this situation: unmanaged packages are used "for distributing open-source projects to developers, or as a one-time drop of applications that require customization after installation". Build the package from the app already running in ETO's org, install it in NTO's org, and the components land as ordinary metadata that NTO's admins can then edit.
The trade the unmanaged route accepts is that the publisher "can't change or upgrade" an unmanaged package after installation - there is no upgrade channel back to ETO. For a one-time transfer of an app NTO is taking ownership of, that is the intended behaviour rather than a loss.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Create users in ETO's org for NTO's sales team) — leaves the sales team working in the wrong system.
Option C (Build a core team and rebuild the app in NTO's org) — the slowest path of all.
Option D (Create a managed package) — the format "used by Salesforce partners to distribute and sell applications to customers", which needs a globally unique namespace registered before anything can be uploaded, and installed managed components are locked against modification, so NTO's own team could not adapt the app they just acquired.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.packagingGuide.meta/packagingGuide/packaging_developing_unmanaged.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pkg1_dev.meta/pkg1_dev/sharing_apps.htm

corrected.note: Answer moved D to A. Salesforce documents the unmanaged package as the one-time drop of an application that is customized after installation, which is this scenario and the fastest route. A managed package targets partner distribution, needs a registered namespace first, and locks its components against edits in the installing org - so it is both slower to produce and wrong for an app NTO will now own and modify.

question: Universal Containers has just acquired Planetary Storage. Both companies use Salesforce to manage their sales activities. The two companies have many customers in common and the company plans to merge the two sales organizations, but the products and sales processes between the two original companies will remain different and distinct. What factor should the company consider in merging the two Salesforce orgs into a single org?
optionA: Transactional sales data could be combined without modification since standard objects are used.
optionB: Business processes on standard objects can be merged without modifications.
optionC: Customer data could be merged with modifications using standardization and de-duplication.
optionD: Salespersons selling both product lines would need two logins, one for each product line.
explanation:
Customer data being mergeable with modifications, using standardization and de-duplication, is the factor to consider. Many shared customers means shared customer records exist in both orgs with conflicting or duplicate data. The merge requires standardization - canonical formats for names, phones, addresses and IDs - and de-duplication through matching rules, duplicate rules and manual review.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Transactional sales data combined without modification) — the products and sales processes differ, so the sales data cannot simply be combined.
Option B (Business processes on standard objects merged without modification) — the stem says the processes will remain different and distinct.
Option D (Two logins per salesperson) — defeats the purpose of merging into a single org.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sales.managing_duplicates_overview.htm&type=5

question: Universal Containers has just initiated a project to implement a custom container tracking application with a large development team. The project manager is concerned that the large number of developers in a single Developer Pro sandbox could lead to challenges with code being overwritten. Which two methods should be used to mitigate this risk? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Replace the Developer Pro sandbox with a Partial Copy sandbox.
optionB: Provide each developer their own sandbox/developer org and implement a code repository and continuous integration to merge code into the Developer Pro sandbox.
optionC: Provide each developer their own sandbox/developer org and implement managed packages to deploy to the merge.
optionD: Use a single sandbox and strictly coordinate development across shared components, and implement a code repository to allow developers to merge code into a common repository.
explanation:
Giving each developer their own sandbox or developer org with a code repository and continuous integration merging into the Developer Pro sandbox, or using a single sandbox with strict coordination over shared components and a common repository, are the two methods. The risk is two developers editing the same component in one org, where the second save silently wins - there is no merge step in a sandbox. The primary answer removes the shared surface: give each developer their own environment, so their work is isolated until they commit, and let the repository and continuous integration perform the merge into the shared Developer Pro sandbox. That is the standard org development arrangement, where each team member customizes in their own Developer sandbox and the source repo becomes the record of what is being delivered.
The fallback answer accepts a single environment but still adds the repository, which is what gives the team a history to recover from and a place to resolve conflicts, plus explicit coordination over the components more than one person touches.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Replace Developer Pro with a Partial Copy) — swapping the sandbox type changes the data it holds and nothing about concurrent editing.
Option C (Own orgs plus managed packages to deploy to the merge) — managed packages are a distribution format, not a mechanism for merging one team's in-progress work with another's.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a huge volume of metadata that cannot be deployed at once. What is the recommended strategy for UC to be successful with the deployment?
optionA: Use a continuous integration tool such as Jenkins to deploy in the right order.
optionB: Identify metadata dependencies, create logical groupings, and deploy in the right order.
optionC: Use a combination of the Ant Migration Tool and change sets for deployment.
optionD: Sort and group the metadata alphabetically and deploy them in the same order.
explanation:
Identifying metadata dependencies, creating logical groupings, and deploying in the right order is the recommended strategy. Large deployments fail because of dependency cycles and ordering, not because of the tool used. Map the dependency graph, partition the metadata into deployable bundles (for example custom objects and fields, then Apex, then page layouts, then reports), and deploy in dependency-respecting order.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (A CI tool such as Jenkins to deploy in order) — a tool can only follow an order someone has already worked out; the choice of tool is secondary.
Option C (Ant Migration Tool plus change sets) — again a tooling choice, and it does nothing about dependencies.
Option D (Sort and group alphabetically) — ignores dependencies entirely.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: Universal Containers is about to begin the release of a major project. To facilitate this, they have several sandboxes to make their deployment train. These sandboxes are a mix of preview and non-preview instances. What should the architect recommend?
optionA: No advice needed, mixing instance types is important for regression testing.
optionB: Refresh all non-preview sandboxes during the release preview window.
optionC: Contact support to roll back the release when Salesforce upgrades the sandboxes.
optionD: Refresh all non-preview sandboxes when the release management team has time.
explanation:
Refreshing all non-preview sandboxes during the release preview window is the recommendation. A preview sandbox sits on an instance that takes the next Salesforce release early; a non-preview sandbox stays on the release production is running. Carrying a deployment train across both means components are built and tested against two different platform versions at once.
The documented lever is the refresh itself. During the transition between major releases Salesforce creates preview sandboxes by default - to get a non-preview sandbox in that window you must have the option enabled by Salesforce support and then explicitly choose Request Non-Preview. So refreshing the non-preview sandboxes inside the preview window is what brings the whole train onto the same release.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (No advice needed, mixing is good for regression) — a train split across two platform versions tests two different things, which is the problem rather than a feature.
Option C (Contact support to roll back the release) — rolling a sandbox back off the new release is not something support does.
Option D (Refresh when the release team has time) — how the split arose in the first place.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers operates from North America and does business within North America. UC has just acquired a local company in Asia to start operating from Asia. Currently, these two business units operate in two different languages. Both units have different sales processes and have to comply strictly with local laws. During the expansion phase, UC would like to focus on innovation over standardization. What should an architect recommend given the scenario?
optionA: Single-org strategy, standardized sales process, common rules, and business-unit-specific locale.
optionB: Multi-org strategy, standardized sales process, common rules, and same locale across orgs.
optionC: Single-org strategy, standardized sales process, common rules, and same locale for all business units.
optionD: Multi-org strategy, each org has its own sales process, common rules, and operates in its own locale.
explanation:
A multi-org strategy where each org has its own sales process, common rules, and operates in its own locale is the recommendation. Every fact in the scenario pushes the same way on Salesforce's operating-model framework for org strategy: different sales processes and a stated preference for innovation over standardization put the business low on standardization, and two units serving separate territories under different local law share no process integration. That is the Diversification quadrant, where the guidance is that these companies "will probably always have multiple orgs" - the work to force different business processes and data models into one org "is usually very complicated".
The three rejected options all standardize the sales process, which is the one thing the business explicitly said it does not want during the expansion phase.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Single org, standardized process, unit-specific locale) — standardizes the sales process against the stated preference for innovation.
Option B (Multi-org, standardized process, same locale) — the right org count with the wrong process decision, and it imposes one locale on units operating in different languages.
Option C (Single org, standardized process, same locale) — standardizes both the process and the locale, the two things the scenario rules out.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers is validating an outbound change set from the Developer sandbox to the production org. Which two locking behaviors will occur during a deployment? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The sandbox org will be locked. Administrators cannot modify metadata.
optionB: The production org will be locked. Users will still be able to read/write data to the org.
optionC: The production org will be locked. Administrators cannot modify metadata during this time.
optionD: The production org will be locked. Users can only read data during this time.
explanation:
The production org is locked so that users can still read and write data, and the production org is locked so that administrators cannot modify metadata, are the two locking behaviours. A deployment takes an org lock on the target, and the lock is over metadata rather than the org as a whole. Salesforce describes the behaviour directly: administrative changes that affect large numbers of records - including metadata deployments - lock the relevant setup area so that simultaneous conflicting changes cannot corrupt data or metadata, and the lock is self-resolving with no manual removal. So an administrator attempting a setup change against production while the deployment runs meets an Org Administration Locked error. Nothing in that stops ordinary work: users keep reading and writing records throughout, which is why a production deployment does not require an outage window for the business.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (The sandbox org is locked) — the source org is not involved; a change set is validated and deployed against the target, so the sandbox it came from stays fully editable.
Option D (Users can only read data) — the lock is on setup, not on records; users keep writing data during the deployment.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000384452&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.changesets_inbound_deploy.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is embarking on a large program of work, with different projects and different vendors. UC created a Center of Excellence (CoE) that is struggling with scope creep between the different projects. What role should the architect suggest be added to the CoE?
optionA: Change Manager
optionB: Release Manager
optionC: Product Owner
optionD: Scrum Master
explanation:
A Change Manager is the role to add. Scope creep between multiple projects and vendors is a cross-project change-control problem, which is the Change Manager's remit within a CoE. The Change Manager owns the change-control process - reviewing, approving, and gatekeeping change requests across the whole program - so they can hold the line on scope across projects rather than within one.
Note: the certification exam treats Change Manager here as change-control governance, not user-adoption change management.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Release Manager) — handles the deployment pipeline, not what is allowed into scope.
Option C (Product Owner) — governs backlog and priorities within a single product or project and has no authority across projects, so it does not address creep between them.
Option D (Scrum Master) — facilitates a single team and has no authority over scope.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Which two decisions should be made by an Architecture Review Board (ARB)? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: What testing tools should be used to track integration testing requirements.
optionB: Whether to utilize the Waterfall or Agile methodology on the project.
optionC: Whether to implement Single Sign-On with SAML or delegated authentication.
optionD: Whether to create a new Salesforce object or override an existing object using a new record type.
explanation:
Whether to implement Single Sign-On with SAML or delegated authentication, and whether to create a new Salesforce object or use a record type on an existing one, are the two ARB decisions. An architecture review board rules on decisions that are expensive to reverse and that constrain everything built afterwards. Choosing between SAML single sign-on and delegated authentication is one: it fixes how identity is established for every user and integration, and unwinding it later touches every connected system. So is deciding whether a requirement becomes a new custom object or a record type on an existing one - that choice propagates into sharing, reporting, automation and every integration that queries the object, and it is very costly to change once data exists.
Note that the division of authority between an ARB and other governance bodies is organizational practice rather than a documented Salesforce rule; the references orient rather than decide it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Which testing tools track integration testing) — a delivery-tooling choice, not an architectural one.
Option B (Waterfall or Agile for the project) — a methodology decision for the sponsor or steering committee; it shapes how the work is organized, not how the system is built.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to implement a release strategy with major releases every four weeks and minor releases every week. Major releases follow Development, System Testing (SIT), User Acceptance Testing (UAT), and Training. Minor releases follow Development and User Acceptance Testing (UAT) stages. What represents a valid environment strategy consideration for UAT?
optionA: Minor and major releases use separate Developer Pro sandboxes.
optionB: Minor and major releases use the same Full Copy sandbox.
optionC: Minor releases use a Partial Copy sandbox and major releases use a Full Copy sandbox.
optionD: Minor releases use a Developer sandbox and major releases use a Full Copy sandbox.
explanation:
Minor releases using a Partial Copy sandbox and major releases using a Full Copy sandbox is the valid UAT consideration. The decisive constraint is the refresh interval, not the size of the release. A Full sandbox can be refreshed only every 29 days, which cannot serve a UAT environment feeding weekly minor releases; a Partial Copy refreshes every 5 days and carries a sample of production data defined by a sandbox template, which is enough to accept a small change. Major releases every four weeks fit the Full sandbox cadence, and they are the ones that need a production-sized, fully populated org to be accepted in.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Separate Developer Pro sandboxes) — Developer Pro copies metadata only, so no business user can run acceptance testing against real data.
Option B (The same Full Copy for both) — a single Full sandbox cannot be refreshed on a weekly rhythm at all.
Option D (Developer sandbox for minor releases) — a Developer sandbox also holds no production data, so it fails UAT for the same reason as option A.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a large backlog of work. They have noticed that despite their best efforts, valuable enhancements and updates are not being completed because they do not have the bandwidth to get them done. Many of these items are low effort and would not require experienced resources. What should the architect recommend that will minimize additional costs and allow UC to accomplish more?
optionA: UC should start a citizen development program.
optionB: UC should eliminate low-value items from the backlog.
optionC: UC should hire additional resources to reduce the backlog.
optionD: UC should hire a partner to complete the needed backlog items.
explanation:
Starting a citizen development program is the recommendation. The constraint is stated in the question: the outstanding items are low effort, do not need experienced resources, and the answer must not add cost. A citizen development programme is the option that adds capacity without adding spend: business users build the low-risk, declarative items themselves inside guard-rails that IT sets - naming and design standards, a review step, a defined boundary for what a citizen developer may touch and what must come to the platform team. The governance is what separates it from ungoverned admin sprawl, and it is the part that has to be designed rather than assumed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Eliminate low-value items from the backlog) — the items are described as valuable enhancements, so this resolves the queue by discarding the value.
Option C (Hire additional resources) — fails the no-additional-cost test directly.
Option D (Hire a partner) — the same cost failure, outsourced.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A technical lead is performing all code reviews for a team and is finding many errors and improvement points. This is delaying the team's deliveries. Which two actions can effectively contribute to the quality and agility of the team? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create development standards and train teams in those standards.
optionB: Choose the most senior developer to help the technical lead in the code review.
optionC: Skip the code review and focus on functional tests and UAT.
optionD: Use a static code analysis tool in the pipeline before manual code review.
explanation:
Creating development standards with training, and using a static code analysis tool in the pipeline before manual review, are the two actions. The bottleneck is one person catching problems that should never have reached them, so both answers move work off that person. Written standards plus training change what developers submit - the recurring findings become habits rather than review comments. A static analyser in the pipeline catches the mechanical half automatically: Salesforce's own Code Analyzer unifies engines such as PMD, RetireJS and ESLint, runs from the CLI so it fits "into your build and deployment processes", and supports custom rules for a team's own conventions. What reaches the technical lead is then design and logic, which is the part that actually needs their judgment.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Add the most senior developer as a second reviewer) — doubles the reviewing capacity without reducing the volume of findings, and removes another experienced developer from delivery.
Option C (Skip code review for functional tests and UAT) — trades a delivery delay for defects found later, at higher cost, by users.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is looking for advice on how often it should refresh its sandboxes. UC currently uses a development lifecycle that starts with developer environments and moves to integration testing, QA testing, UAT, and then production. They have many scrum teams working concurrently and the teams do not agree on when refreshes should occur. What two recommendations should the architect suggest? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Integration sandboxes should be refreshed rarely because of the burden of maintaining the various API connections.
optionB: Sandboxes should be refreshed on the day when the refresh is allowed for that type of sandbox.
optionC: Development environments should generally be refreshed after each working feature has been successfully migrated.
optionD: Production is the only pristine environment.
explanation:
Development environments being refreshed after each working feature has been successfully migrated, and production being the only pristine environment, are the two recommendations - both come straight from Salesforce's environment-management guidance. Of the developer sandboxes it says: "I typically expect these sandboxes to be refreshed after a working feature has been successfully migrated upstream" - so a developer starts each new piece of work from the state that was just proven upstream. And it states the governing principle for every other environment: production is your only pristine environment, which is why refreshes only ever flow from production outward and every downstream org is understood to be drifting.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Refresh integration sandboxes rarely because of API connections) — the same source rejects this: it recommends refreshing the system integration sandbox "as often as is practical", and for that reason advises against using a Full sandbox there, since its 29-day refresh limit is too slow.
Option B (Refresh on the first day the interval allows) — lets the calendar rather than the delivery pipeline decide.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation conceded that the integration-sandbox option "is sometimes argued" and that frequent integration refreshes break partner connections. The source it rests on says the opposite: refresh the system integration sandbox as often as is practical, and avoid a Full sandbox there precisely because 29 days is too infrequent.

question: Cloud Kicks is considering using an automated testing tool to help manage deployments between environments. When should the architect recommend the use of an automated testing tool?
optionA: Automated tests should be run daily in all developer orgs.
optionB: Automated tests should be run only when merging into Full or Partial Copy sandboxes.
optionC: Automated tests should be run daily in all developer orgs, and when branches are merged.
optionD: Automated tests should be run when branches are merged.
explanation:
Running automated tests daily in all developer orgs and when branches are merged is the recommendation. Best practice is to run automated tests both as a scheduled daily build, which catches environment drift, scheduled-job interactions and regressions, and on every merge to the integration branch, which gates broken code from reaching shared environments.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Daily in developer orgs only) — half the practice; nothing gates a merge.
Option B (Only when merging into Full or Partial Copy sandboxes) — restricting tests to the higher sandboxes lets bugs accumulate at the lower tiers.
Option D (Only when branches are merged) — the other half; drift and scheduled-job regressions between merges go unseen.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html

question: Universal Containers (UC) is developing a new Customer Community. Requirements for the Community are not fully defined. UC is planning on using an Agile methodology for this work and has promised delivery of the complete system in three months. What are two risks associated with this approach? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Agile does not allow for changes to requirements, so customers might not like the resulting solution.
optionB: Agile is not an appropriate development methodology for Customer Community implementations.
optionC: Given the lack of requirements and the three-month timeline commitment, the project may not be feasible.
optionD: The functionality that can be delivered in 3 months is unknown, and may not meet the needs of the business.
explanation:
The project possibly not being feasible given the lack of requirements and the three-month commitment, and the deliverable functionality being unknown and possibly not meeting the business's needs, are the two risks. Agile flexes scope against a fixed time and cost, and this commitment has removed the flex while leaving the scope undefined. Nobody can say today whether a complete system is achievable in three months, because there is no agreed definition of complete - so the feasibility of the promise is unknown rather than optimistic. And whatever does fit inside the window will be decided by prioritization as the work proceeds, which means the delivered functionality may not be the functionality the business needed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Agile does not allow requirement changes) — wrong about Agile; changing requirements is what the method is designed to accommodate, and the Agile Manifesto values "responding to change over following a plan".
Option B (Agile is inappropriate for Customer Communities) — nothing about a customer community makes it unsuitable for iterative delivery.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers has decided on a single-org strategy, despite having to deal with the complexity of having multiple lines of business (LOBs) inside a single org. What are two common challenges in a single-org strategy for multiple LOBs? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Lack of declarative sharing and visibility capabilities to ensure correct visibility of objects and records.
optionB: Making Salesforce work with multiple currencies.
optionC: Apex design will need to be mature and adhere to strict guidelines to support a large enterprise model.
optionD: The data model becomes more complex as the scope in the org increases.
explanation:
Apex design needing to be mature and adhere to strict guidelines, and the data model becoming more complex as the org's scope grows, are the two challenges Salesforce's own org-strategy guidance names for a single org serving many lines of business: "Your data model becomes much more complex and controversial as you increase your scope in the org", and "Your apex design will need to be very mature to support a large enterprise model" - every line of business shares one execution context, so trigger frameworks, governor limits and separation of concerns have to be engineered rather than left to convention.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Lack of declarative sharing and visibility capabilities) — sharing and visibility are configured declaratively through the role hierarchy, sharing rules and territories; the platform handles this well.
Option B (Making Salesforce work with multiple currencies) — multi-currency is a standard org setting with dated exchange rates, not a single-org challenge.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers (UC) operates globally from different geographical locations. UC is revisiting their current org strategy. Which three factors should an architect consider for a single-org strategy? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Consistent processes across the business.
optionB: Increased ability to collaborate.
optionC: Fewer interdependencies.
optionD: Centralized data location.
explanation:
Consistent processes across the business, increased ability to collaborate, and a centralized data location are the three factors that favour a single org: the business runs consistent processes everywhere so one configuration fits all, collaboration across regions is high so one org means one Chatter and one search, and centralized data gives a single 360-degree view of every customer.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Fewer interdependencies) — argues for multi-org; separate orgs are what reduce interdependencies.
Option E (Tailored implementation) — also a multi-org argument, since a single org standardizes rather than tailors.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a large user base (>300 users) and was originally implemented eight years ago by a Salesforce systems integration partner. Since then, UC has made a number of changes to their Visualforce pages and Apex classes in response to customer requirements, made by a variety of vendors and internal teams. Which three issues would a new technical architect expect to see when evaluating the code in the Salesforce org? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Custom-built JSON and string manipulation classes that are no longer required.
optionB: Multiple unit test failures would be encountered.
optionC: Broken functionality due to Salesforce upgrades.
optionD: Multiple triggers on the same object, making it hard to understand the order of operations.
optionE: Duplicated logic across Visualforce pages and Apex classes performing similar tasks.
explanation:
Custom-built JSON and string manipulation classes that are no longer required, multiple triggers on the same object, and duplicated logic across Visualforce pages and Apex classes are the three issues to expect. Eight years of changes by rotating vendors produces accretion, and the three keyed findings are its structural signatures. Hand-rolled JSON and string-parsing utilities are redundant because Apex has native support - System.JSON serializes and deserializes Apex objects directly, with createParser and createGenerator for lower-level work - so code predating that survives as dead weight. Multiple triggers on one object is the classic consequence of successive teams each adding their own rather than extending what exists, and the platform gives no guarantee about the order in which they fire. And logic duplicated across Visualforce pages and Apex classes is what happens when each vendor builds beside the previous work instead of refactoring it.
A caution about the two options this item excludes: they are not impossible, only not the findings you would predict from this history.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Multiple unit test failures) — common in long-lived orgs, but usually because tests depend on org data or hardcoded ids, not a structural signature of vendor accretion.
Option C (Broken functionality from Salesforce upgrades) — Salesforce's versioning commitment applies to code pinned to an API version; it is not a promise that an upgrade can never affect behaviour, which is why release preview windows and regression testing exist, but it is not what this history predicts.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_class_System_Json.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation ruled out two options by claiming Salesforce's backward-compatibility guarantee means platform upgrades never break existing unit tests. That is not what versioning promises, and it contradicts two other questions in this deck, which key on refreshing into the release preview window and regression testing an upgraded sandbox precisely because a release can break existing behaviour.

question: Which are two characteristics of an effective communication plan? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Consistent communication to a pre-defined list of stakeholders.
optionB: Communication to stakeholders on a 'need-to-know' basis.
optionC: Requesting feedback for outstanding architectural questions.
optionD: Reporting project status, timelines, and impacts.
explanation:
Consistent communication to a pre-defined list of stakeholders, and reporting project status, timelines and impacts, are the two characteristics. A communication plan is judged on predictability and content. Predictability means a named list of stakeholders who each know what they will receive and when, so nobody has to ask and nobody is surprised. Content means the substance stakeholders need to make decisions - status against plan, timelines, and the impacts of what has changed since the last update, including the bad news.
Note that this is communication practice rather than a platform fact; the reference is orienting rather than decisive.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Need-to-know communication) — makes each disclosure a judgment call by the sender, which produces exactly the surprises that erode trust.
Option C (Requesting feedback on open architectural questions) — real design work carried out with specific people, not a property of the plan that keeps stakeholders informed.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers has just initiated a project involving a large distributed development and testing team. The development team members need access to a tool to manage requirements, and the testing team needs access to a tool to manage defects. Additionally, stakeholders are requesting ad-hoc status reports. What tool should an architect recommend to support the project?
optionA: Wave (Tableau CRM)
optionB: Code Repository
optionC: Spreadsheets
optionD: Project Management Tool
explanation:
A Project Management Tool is the recommendation. Three needs are described - requirements for the developers, defects for the testers, and ad hoc status for stakeholders - and they are three views of the same underlying work items. A project management tool holds all of them in one place, which matters most for a distributed team: the requirement, the defect raised against it, and the status report drawn from both stay connected without anyone reconciling separate systems.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Wave / Tableau CRM) — an analytics platform reports on data it is given and does not capture the work.
Option B (Code Repository) — versions the source and can link a commit to a work item, but it does not manage requirements or defect workflow.
Option C (Spreadsheets) — can hold a list, but have no workflow, no concurrent editing discipline for a distributed team, and no live status for stakeholders to pull.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers is in the process of testing their integration between Salesforce and their on-premise ERP systems. The testing team has requested a sandbox with up to 10,000 records in each object to benchmark the integration performance. What is the fastest approach an architect should recommend?
optionA: Spin off a Developer sandbox, migrate the metadata, and load the data using Data Loader.
optionB: Spin off a Full Copy sandbox with all the objects that are required for testing the integration.
optionC: Spin off a Developer Pro sandbox, migrate the metadata, and load the data using Data Loader.
optionD: Spin off a Partial Copy sandbox using a sandbox template with all the objects required for testing the integration.
explanation:
Spinning off a Partial Copy sandbox using a sandbox template with the objects required for the integration test is the fastest approach. The requirement names the Partial Copy sandbox's documented limit almost exactly: a Partial Copy carries "standard and custom object records and Attachments up to 5 GB, with a maximum of 10,000 records per selected object", with the objects chosen through a sandbox template. So the testing team's 10,000 records per object arrive automatically on creation, with no data load to build or run.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Developer sandbox plus Data Loader) — Developer sandboxes copy metadata only, so this ends in a manual Data Loader run for every object.
Option B (Full Copy sandbox) — would hold the data, but copies the entire production database and takes far longer to provision and refresh; the question asks for the fastest approach.
Option C (Developer Pro sandbox plus Data Loader) — metadata only as well, with the same manual load.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000381868&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.data_sandbox_templates.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is considering updating their Salesforce release management process. Which three best practices should UC consider for version control? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Maintain a single entry point for production from the master branch.
optionB: Maintain unrestricted access to the release sandboxes for all changes being deployed.
optionC: Maintain separate developer branches for minor and major releases.
optionD: Automation is a must with various application branches in the repository.
optionE: Maintain a single repository for the application with individual branches for projects.
explanation:
Maintaining a single entry point for production from the master branch, separate developer branches for minor and major releases, and a single repository for the application with individual project branches are the three version-control best practices. One trunk or main branch is the single source of truth for production deploys; separate branches isolate minor (fast-track) and major (longer-running) work so they do not entangle; and one repository per application with a branch per project keeps related artifacts together.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Unrestricted access to release sandboxes) — the opposite of governance, and not a version-control practice at all.
Option D (Automation is a must with various branches) — true in general, but a pipeline statement rather than a version-control practice.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses a managed package to install an internal Sales app in five orgs. Within each org there are integrations and local processes with the objects of the managed package. UC wants to use unlocked packages for better integration with CI/CD processes. What would the Salesforce architect recommend for this migration?
optionA: Export all data from objects/fields of the managed package, uninstall it, install an unlocked package with the same namespace as the managed package, and restore all data.
optionB: Export all data from objects/fields of the managed package, uninstall it, install the unlocked package without a namespace, and restore all data.
optionC: Do not change to unlocked packages, as it is possible to perform all CI/CD processes with the managed package.
optionD: Migrate all classes, Visualforce, and components from the managed package to the unlocked package. Install the new version of the managed package (objects/fields only) and the unlocked package with the other components.
explanation:
Migrating the classes, Visualforce and components from the managed package to an unlocked package, then installing the new managed package version (objects and fields only) alongside the unlocked package, is the recommendation. The two options that begin by uninstalling are disqualified by what uninstalling costs. Salesforce's own conversion procedure spells out the sequence - export all the data from the package's objects, uninstall it, install the replacement, and import the data back - and across five orgs carrying live integrations and local processes built on those objects, that is a destructive migration, not a tooling change.
That leaves splitting the package by layer: leave the data model where it is, so the objects, fields and every integration and local customization bound to them keep their identity, and move the classes, pages and components into an unlocked package that can be built from source on every commit.
Plan the removal carefully, because taking components out of a released managed package is a controlled operation rather than a simple edit - Salesforce supports removing metadata components from second-generation managed packages through a documented process, and in most cases removal marks the component deprecated rather than hard-deleting it from subscriber orgs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Export, uninstall, install an unlocked package with the same namespace, restore) — a destructive export-uninstall-reimport across five live orgs, and an unlocked package cannot simply reuse the managed package's namespace to preserve identity.
Option B (Export, uninstall, install without a namespace, restore) — the same destructive migration, and every integration and local process bound to the namespaced objects breaks.
Option C (Stay on the managed package) — doing nothing is not an answer, since the goal is to bring the code under CI/CD.

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pkg2_dev.meta/pkg2_dev/sfdx_dev_dev2gp_remove_md_components.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has well-defined release management processes for both large and small projects. NTO's development team created a workflow and a trigger for changes in its opportunity renewal process. What should the architect recommend for release planning of these changes?
optionA: Plan this as an interim release after checking with Salesforce Support.
optionB: Plan this as a major release and align with a Salesforce major release.
optionC: Plan this as a minor release with training and change management.
optionD: Plan this as a patch release and align with a Salesforce patch release.
explanation:
Planning this as a minor release with training and change management is the recommendation. Size the release to the change. A workflow rule and a trigger on the opportunity renewal process is a small, well-bounded piece of work, so it belongs in the minor release stream rather than being held for a major one. What it is not is invisible: it changes what sales users see when they renew an opportunity, so it needs training and change communication to go with it. That pairing - minor release, real change management - is what the answer captures.
Currency note: Workflow Rules reached end of support at the end of 2025, with Flow as the replacement, so equivalent automation built today would be a record-triggered flow.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Interim release after checking with Salesforce Support) — Support has no role in a customer's release planning, and an interim category is not a real planning option here.
Option B (Major release aligned with a Salesforce major release) — delays a small change for months, and lands the org's change at the same moment as the platform's, so any defect is harder to attribute; Salesforce upgrades are not a release slot a customer can book.
Option D (Patch release aligned with a Salesforce patch) — Salesforce patches arrive on Salesforce's schedule, not the customer's, so there is nothing to align to.
References:
