https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What is the responsibility of the technical architect within a Change Control Board meeting?
optionA: Approve the upcoming release for deployment into production.
optionB: Prioritize the Salesforce product roadmap with business stakeholders.
optionC: Troubleshoot deployment errors that occurred during the last release.
optionD: Conduct code reviews for projects in the development phase.
explanation:
Approving the upcoming release for deployment into production is the technical architect's responsibility at a Change Control Board. A change control board exists to decide whether a change may proceed, and each seat brings one kind of authority to that decision. The technical architect's is technical: whether the release is sound enough to go to production - its design, its risk, its dependencies, its rollback path - and the meeting is where that judgment is recorded as an approval or a rejection.
The three rejected activities are all real architect work happening somewhere else.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Prioritize the product roadmap with stakeholders) — a planning forum, not a control board.
Option C (Troubleshoot last release's deployment errors) — incident work that may produce input to this meeting but is not conducted in it.
Option D (Conduct code reviews) — belongs in the development flow, well before a release reaches a control board; if code quality is first examined at the CCB, the gate is in the wrong place.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers wants to do weekly releases to production. What approach will mitigate the risk of bugs being inadvertently introduced to production?
optionA: Use of an Agile methodology.
optionB: Automated testing.
optionC: User acceptance testing.
optionD: Requirements traceability.
explanation:
Automated testing is the approach. Weekly releases require a regression suite that runs in minutes, not days. Automated testing - unit, integration and UI smoke - gates each release in a CI pipeline, blocking regressions before they reach production.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Agile methodology) — sets the cadence but does not catch bugs.
Option C (User acceptance testing) — manual UAT cannot scale to a weekly cadence.
Option D (Requirements traceability) — tracing links requirements to work; it does not detect a regression.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_code_coverage_intro.htm

question: Which two project situations favor a Waterfall methodology? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: An application in post-production, with incremental changes made by a small team.
optionB: An application with many systems and inter-dependencies between components.
optionC: An application with regulatory compliance requirements to be validated by outside agencies.
optionD: An in-house application with a fixed team size, but an open timeline and flexible requirements.
explanation:
An application with many systems and inter-dependencies between components, and one with regulatory compliance requirements validated by outside agencies, are the two situations that favour Waterfall. Waterfall pays for itself when the cost of getting the design wrong is higher than the cost of designing it all first. Many systems with dependencies between components is one such case - interfaces, data flows and sequencing have to be agreed across teams before anyone builds, because a late change in one component ripples through the others. Regulatory requirements validated by an outside agency is the other: the phase artefacts and traceable documentation Waterfall produces are the evidence the validation runs on, and an iterative process that leaves that documentation until later has nothing to submit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Post-production app with incremental changes by a small team) — where iterating is cheap; the team can ship, learn and adjust continuously.
Option D (In-house app, fixed team, open timeline, flexible requirements) — has no fixed baseline for Waterfall to protect, so change is expected rather than costly.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) has received feedback from the field on several new feature requests aligned to business goals. UC is looking for a way to quickly get feedback and prioritize these requests. Which two options should an architect recommend? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create the backlog or priority list in a project management tool.
optionB: Present the feature requests at a Center of Excellence meeting.
optionC: Send the requests to IT for a formal review at the end of the year.
optionD: Bring the feature request to the Test Manager to gain quality checks.
optionE: Create design standards around the new features being requested.
explanation:
Creating the backlog or priority list in a project management tool, and presenting the feature requests at a Center of Excellence meeting, are the two options. Prioritization needs a list and a forum, and the two keyed options supply one each. A single backlog in a project management tool is what lets requests be compared against each other rather than each being argued on its own merits as it arrives. The centre of excellence is where that ranking is decided against business goals by people with the standing to decide it - Salesforce's org-strategy guidance describes the CoE as the body that manages business architecture and common standards across the enterprise, which is the authority this needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Formal IT review at the end of the year) — the opposite of quick feedback.
Option D (Bring requests to the Test Manager for quality checks) — quality checks govern how a request is built once accepted, not whether it should be.
Option E (Create design standards around the requested features) — the same: a build-time control, not a prioritization step.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers has a highly integrated environment with significant process orchestration between systems. When refreshing UAT, objects that have External IDs from production no longer point to valid External IDs in the UAT environment. What should an architect do to resolve this?
optionA: Let UAT point to production integrations and roll back each transaction after it finishes.
optionB: Delete all the data and use an automated testing tool to create new data across all the systems in UAT.
optionC: Mask the External ID so nobody can see the production value.
optionD: In the post-refresh plan, modify External IDs to a known valid set of values for UAT.
explanation:
Modifying the External IDs to a known valid set of values for UAT in the post-refresh plan is what the architect should do. A refresh copies production values wholesale, so every External ID in the refreshed org still names a record in the connected production systems. Left alone, UAT orchestration reaches straight back into production-equivalent records - which is why rewriting those identifiers belongs in the post-refresh plan alongside endpoints, credentials and named credentials.
Salesforce provides the hook for it: an Apex class implementing the SandboxPostCopy interface runs "at the end of the sandbox copy using a special Automated Process user", and the documented uses are exactly this kind of preparation - create users, "run sanitizing code on records", and perform other setup tasks. Scripting the External ID remap there makes it repeatable on every refresh rather than a manual step someone forgets.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Point UAT at production integrations and roll back each transaction) — this is the risk itself, not a mitigation.
Option B (Delete all data and generate new data with a testing tool) — throws away the production-like shape the refresh was for.
Option C (Mask the External ID) — only hides the value from users; the integration still sends it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_interface_System_SandboxPostCopy.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What are two advantages of automated test data loads over manual data loads? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Automated loads can be done with no human oversight.
optionB: Automated loads are reliable in their results.
optionC: Automated loads will increase costs.
optionD: Automated loads cannot be scripted by CI/CD tools.
explanation:
Automated loads running with no human oversight, and being reliable in their results, are the two advantages. Once scripted, automated loads run unattended - overnight, on schedule, in CI - with no operator required, and they produce identical, repeatable results every run, which is a key property for testing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Automated loads increase costs) — a disadvantage if it were true, not an advantage; scripting a load is a one-off cost that repays itself on every run.
Option D (Cannot be scripted by CI/CD tools) — false; CI/CD tools script Data Loader and Bulk API operations routinely.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_load_data.htm

question: The team at Universal Containers is building an application on Java that will interact with its Salesforce application. They want to use SOQL queries to retrieve and make changes to smaller pieces of Salesforce metadata through this application. Which API should the team leverage?
optionA: Tooling API
optionB: User Interface API
optionC: Metadata API
optionD: Any Salesforce API
explanation:
The Tooling API is the one to leverage, because the requirement names its defining feature. Salesforce describes it as giving "fine-grained access to an org's metadata", where "Tooling API's SOQL capabilities for many metadata types allow you to retrieve smaller pieces of metadata" and "smaller retrieves improve performance, which makes Tooling API a better fit for developing interactive applications" - which is precisely a Java application querying and amending individual metadata components.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (User Interface API) — returns records and the layout information needed to render them, not metadata definitions.
Option C (Metadata API) — works the other way: deploy() and retrieve() "move metadata (XML files) between a Salesforce org and a local file system" in bulk, with no SOQL against metadata at all.
Option D (Any Salesforce API) — only the Tooling API exposes metadata to SOQL, so the choice is not interchangeable.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_tooling.meta/api_tooling/intro_api_tooling.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: What is the responsibility of an executive sponsor on a project?
optionA: Communicate project status.
optionB: Determine project methodology.
optionC: Approve changes to project scope.
optionD: Design executive dashboards.
explanation:
Approving changes to project scope is the executive sponsor's responsibility. The executive sponsor owns the project's business case and its funding, and scope is what connects those two things - a change to scope changes the cost, the date, or the benefit being claimed. So approving scope changes is the responsibility that follows directly from what the sponsor holds.
Note that role definitions of this kind are organizational practice rather than a documented Salesforce rule; the reference is orienting rather than decisive.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Communicate project status) — the project manager's job; the sponsor is one of its recipients.
Option B (Determine project methodology) — a delivery decision, made against criteria the governance bodies set.
Option D (Design executive dashboards) — implementation work a sponsor may commission but does not perform.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers is about to begin development work on a new project in their Salesforce org that will take many months to complete. UC is concerned about how critical bugs will be addressed for existing live functionality. What is the recommended release management strategy to address this concern?
optionA: Include fixes for critical bugs in the ongoing development sandboxes so that they will be released with the other code.
optionB: Utilize a dedicated Developer Pro sandbox to address critical bugs and release to production.
optionC: Address critical bugs in the development sandboxes and push those changes to production separately.
optionD: Keep teams separate until the end of the project and create a Full Copy sandbox to merge their work then.
explanation:
Utilizing a dedicated Developer Pro sandbox to address critical bugs and release them to production is the recommended strategy. A long-running project and a production defect move on different clocks, so they need different paths to production. Salesforce's environment-management guidance names a dedicated environment for exactly this - a production fix sandbox generated for urgent defects only, holding the minimum needed to reproduce and correct the problem. The fix is built and tested there, deploys to production on its own, and is then merged back into the project work so the long-running branch picks it up.
Every alternative couples the two.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Fix bugs in the ongoing development sandboxes for release with the other code) — the fix cannot ship until the project does, which is months away.
Option C (Fix in the development sandboxes and push separately) — sounds targeted, but drags whatever else that sandbox contains toward production, since the environment holds months of unfinished work.
Option D (Keep teams separate and merge in a Full Copy at the end) — postpones every integration problem to the worst possible moment.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which statement is true for a Staging sandbox in a typical release pipeline?
optionA: Salesforce major releases (e.g., Winter to Spring) always occur in Staging and Production at the same time.
optionB: The Staging environment can only be updated once every two weeks.
optionC: The Staging sandbox is automatically refreshed on a schedule set by the administrator.
optionD: When created or refreshed, the Staging sandbox is a full replica of Production.
explanation:
The Staging sandbox being a full replica of Production when created or refreshed is the true statement. Salesforce names staging as a Full sandbox use case directly: the Full sandbox is "intended to be used as a testing environment" supporting "performance testing, load testing, and staging", and it is "a replica of your production org, including all data, such as object records and attachments, and metadata". So at the moment it is created or refreshed, a staging sandbox mirrors production - which is the whole point of the final pre-production rehearsal.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Major releases always hit Staging and Production together) — a sandbox can sit on a preview instance and take the next major release weeks ahead of production.
Option B (Updated only once every two weeks) — the interval that governs a Full sandbox is 29 days, not two weeks.
Option C (Automatically refreshed on an admin-set schedule) — there is no administrator-scheduled auto-refresh; a refresh is requested manually.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing a governance framework and has asked the architect to make recommendations regarding release planning. Which two decisions should the architect make when planning for releases? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Whether Salesforce will wait to upgrade the pod until after a UC release is complete.
optionB: When to test a new UC feature release if there are issues.
optionC: How to test existing functionality to ensure no regressions are introduced.
optionD: How to roll back to the previous Salesforce release if there are issues.
explanation:
When to test a new UC feature release if there are issues, and how to test existing functionality to prevent regressions, are the two decisions. Release planning decides what the team will do, so both keyed decisions are about the team's own process: when a feature release gets retested if defects are found, and how existing functionality is regression tested so the release does not break what already works. Those are choices with real trade-offs - the size of the regression suite, what is automated, how much re-test a late fix triggers - and nobody else can make them.
The two rejected options ask for control the customer does not have. Salesforce upgrades its instances on its own schedule, and the customer-facing lever is the preview window - a preview sandbox "provides early access to new features and lets you test your configurations before the production upgrade" - which is a way to get ahead of the upgrade rather than to postpone it. Plan around the upgrade calendar; do not plan to move it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Whether Salesforce will wait to upgrade the pod) — Salesforce upgrades on its own schedule; the customer cannot postpone it.
Option D (How to roll back to the previous Salesforce release) — there is no route to roll a Salesforce release back.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is working with Salesforce CPQ, which uses configuration sObjects to drive business logic. What are two best-practice recommendations an architect should propose to allow UC to deploy CPQ features as part of their CI/CD process? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use Data Loader to deploy CSV files.
optionB: Build an Apex framework to deploy CPQ records.
optionC: Use a third-party product (e.g., Prodly, Copado).
optionD: Use an open-source SFDX plugin (e.g., sfdmu) and version control.
explanation:
Using a third-party product such as Prodly or Copado, and using an open-source SFDX plugin such as sfdmu with version control, are the two best-practice recommendations. The obstacle is that CPQ's behaviour is configured in records - product rules, price rules, option and constraint records on managed-package objects - and the Metadata API moves "metadata (XML files) between a Salesforce org and a local file system". Records are outside its remit entirely, so no amount of change-set or package work carries a CPQ configuration between orgs.
That pushes the answer toward tooling built for relationship-aware reference data: a commercial deployer, or an open-source SFDX data plugin driven from the same pipeline with the configuration held in version control. Either way the configuration becomes a reviewable, replayable artefact rather than a manual rebuild per environment.
Note that the specific products named here are practitioner tooling rather than a Salesforce recommendation - what the documentation settles is why the native deployment path cannot do this job.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Data Loader with CSV files) — manual CSV loads break on the lookups between these objects, since every parent record acquires a new Id in the target org.
Option B (An Apex framework to deploy CPQ records) — recreates that same mapping problem as code the team then has to maintain.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet.meta/salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet/salesforce_app_limits_platform_metadata.htm

question: An architect is working on a Universal Containers project, and due to security concerns they cannot provide the architect with production access. Instead, a central release management team will be responsible for performing production deployments for all development teams. How should an architect leverage the Metadata API to ensure any metadata components necessary to deploy the project's functionality are properly communicated to the release management team?
optionA: Create a change set in each sandbox and download the package.xml file for the release management team.
optionB: Provide a spreadsheet of all components and utilize the Metadata API's readMetadata call.
optionC: Send a package.xml file with associated metadata in a .zip file to the release management team.
optionD: Provide the release management team a copy of the audit trail from the sandbox you wish to deploy from.
explanation:
Sending a package.xml file with the associated metadata in a .zip file to the release management team is how to leverage the Metadata API. What the release team needs is something they can deploy without touching the architect's environment, and the Metadata API defines exactly that artefact: deploy() and retrieve() "move metadata (XML files) between a Salesforce org and a local file system", where the payload is a .zip containing the component files plus a package.xml manifest naming them and the API version. Hand over that pair and the team can validate and deploy it into production with any Metadata API client.
The alternatives are not deployable artefacts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Change set per sandbox, download its package.xml) — a change set lives inside the org that created it and cannot be exported to another org's inbound list; a manifest alone carries no components.
Option B (Spreadsheet of components plus readMetadata) — readMetadata reads a component's definition one type at a time and produces nothing installable, and a spreadsheet of names still leaves someone to assemble the payload by hand.
Option D (A copy of the sandbox audit trail) — a log of what changed, not the changes themselves.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

question: Universal Containers has started building a customer Lightning community that contains a few dozen Aura components. The development team lead has come to the Salesforce architect about questions regarding testing the Lightning components. What two knowledge points can the architect pass to the development team lead? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: There is a $T test helper object that can be used to create the instance of the Lightning component, and it is promise enabled.
optionB: The testing can be viewed in the lightning.force.com/c/jasminetests.app URL. The page loads and runs Jasmine tests and writes pass/fail information to the screen.
optionC: The testing of the JavaScript part of the Aura component can be tested in the Jest framework and the Apex controllers can be tested using test classes.
optionD: Install the Lightning test service AppExchange package to enable the Aura component testing.
explanation:
The $T test helper object that creates a promise-enabled instance of the component, and the jasminetests.app page that loads and runs Jasmine tests and writes pass/fail to the screen, are the two knowledge points - both describe the Lightning Testing Service, which is what this item is built on. LTS wrapped standard JavaScript frameworks for Aura, exposed a $T helper object for creating and retrieving component instances asynchronously, and ran its suite from a test app in the org whose page reported pass and fail results on screen.
Read this item as history rather than instruction. Salesforce now states plainly: "We used to recommend Lightning Testing Service (LTS) but it's deprecated and no longer supported." The current recommendations for testing Lightning components are Jest, UTAM, Jasmine, Mocha, Selenium and WebdriverIO. A team standing up component testing today should choose from that list and should not install LTS, whatever this item's key says.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Jest for the Aura JavaScript, test classes for Apex) — Jest belongs to Lightning Web Components rather than Aura, which is why pairing Jest with Aura is the odd one out on this item as written.
Option D (Install the Lightning Testing Service AppExchange package) — LTS was distributed as an unmanaged package rather than an AppExchange listing, and it is now deprecated and should not be installed at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/lightning_testing_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/accessibility_write_tests.htm
