Salesforce's own guide now says the Lightning Testing Service "is deprecated and no longer supported", and points to Jest, UTAM, Jasmine, Mocha, Selenium and WebdriverIO instead. Do not act on this item's advice to install LTS.

question: Which two project situations favor an Agile methodology? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: A digitization project to update an existing customer-facing process and enable quick adjustments.
optionB: A project with well-defined requirements and complex interactions between front- and back-end systems.
optionC: An environment with a heavy investment in DevOps capabilities for rapid testing and deployment.
optionD: A project to be executed by a third party, with a fixed and formal scope, budget, and timeline.
explanation:
A digitization project updating a customer-facing process to enable quick adjustments, and an environment with heavy DevOps investment for rapid testing and deployment, are the two situations that favour Agile. Agile suits work whose right answer emerges from use. Updating a customer-facing process so it can be adjusted quickly is exactly that - the requirement is to keep changing it, and the Agile Manifesto's "responding to change over following a plan" describes the operating model that supports it. The second situation is the enabler rather than the motivation: heavy investment in DevOps means automated testing and fast, repeatable deployment, and without that machinery short iterations collapse under their own release overhead. Agile cadence is only sustainable when shipping is cheap.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Well-defined requirements with complex front-to-back interactions) — a fixed baseline that rewards designing the interfaces up front, which is Waterfall's case.
Option D (Third party with fixed scope, budget and timeline) — contracted against a specification, which is the arrangement Waterfall exists to serve.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) had added a Service team to the Salesforce Platform. The Service team would like to have a few dozen of the service centers entered into the system as technical reference data. The service centers are made searchable in many different web forms and are rather independent from all other business entities. In the past, they had to manually add any new service centers in each sandbox in the code migration path. They would like to eliminate the manual work if possible. What is an optimal way to accomplish this requirement?
optionA: Add the service centers to a list custom settings.
optionB: Define a brand-new custom object with a picklist field to host all of the service centers.
optionC: Add all of the service centers to a custom metadata type.
optionD: Add the service centers to a hierarchical custom settings.
explanation:
Adding all of the service centers to a custom metadata type is the optimal way. The complaint is the manual re-entry in every sandbox, and that is decided by whether the records are metadata or data. Custom metadata type records are metadata: the type and its records travel together through change sets, packages and the Metadata API, so a new service centre is entered once and arrives in every environment with the next deployment. They are also queryable in SOQL, which is what the web forms need.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (List custom settings) — the definition is metadata but the records are data, so someone must populate them again in each org, which is exactly the manual work to be eliminated.
Option B (A new custom object with a picklist field) — the same data problem, plus a data model for reference data that never changes at run time.
Option D (Hierarchical custom settings) — fails on the same point as list custom settings; the values do not deploy.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custommetadatatypes_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_custommetadatatypes.htm

question: Universal Containers uses multiple Salesforce orgs for its different lines of business (LOBs). In a recent analysis, the architect found that UC could have a more complete view of its customers by gathering customer data from different orgs. What two options can an architect recommend to accomplish the customer 360-degree view? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Migrate from multi-org to single-org strategy, consolidating customer data in the process.
optionB: Implement a Hub-and-Spoke multi-org strategy by consolidating customer data in a single org, which will be the master of customer data, and using integration strategies to let the LOB orgs read and write from it.
optionC: Implement a Single Package multi-org strategy by developing and deploying to all orgs a managed package which reads and consolidates customer 360-degree view from the different orgs.
optionD: Implement a Complete Graph multi-org strategy by allowing each org to connect directly to every other, reading and writing customer data from the orgs where it has been originally created.
explanation:
A Hub-and-Spoke multi-org strategy with a single customer-master org that the LOB orgs read and write through integration, and a Complete Graph multi-org strategy where each org connects directly to every other, are the two options. Hub-and-spoke is the pattern Salesforce actually endorses for this: one org holds the customer master and the line-of-business orgs integrate to it, and the org-strategy guidance notes that "using a hub/spoke or reporting hub can also help you achieve your Customer 360 requirements". The complete-graph topology reaches a 360 view by a different route - every org integrates directly with every other and reads customer data where it was created - which is why it is the second keyed option.
Be careful with that second one in practice. The same guidance warns where point-to-point multi-org integration ends up: "before too long you have a spider web of integrations, data replication, and very brittle point-to-point connections". It is a recognised topology, not a recommended one, and its cost grows with the square of the org count.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Migrate to a single org, consolidating customer data) — would also deliver a 360 view, which is why this item is weak; as keyed it tests which of the three named multi-org topologies can deliver one, and a single-org migration abandons the multi-org strategy the stem describes.
Option C (Single Package strategy with a managed package that consolidates the view) — cannot work at all: a managed package distributes metadata and code to each org and does not federate live records across org boundaries, so installing it everywhere leaves the customer data exactly as scattered as before.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

corrected.note: Answer stands, but the item is weak. The old explanation presented the complete-graph topology as simply "suitable when ownership stays distributed"; Salesforce's own org-strategy guidance describes that architecture as a brittle point-to-point spider web. Consolidating into a single org - the first distractor - also delivers a 360 view, so this item is really testing which of three named multi-org topologies can deliver one, not which approach is best.

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to shorten their deployment time to production by controlling which tests to run in production. UC's Architect has suggested that they run only subsets of tests. Which two statements are true regarding running specific tests during deployments? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Specifying the test method is not supported in DeployOptions, therefore specify only the test classes that are required to be executed.
optionB: To run a subset of tests, set the Run Specified Tests test level on the DeployOptions object and pass it as an argument to the deploy() call.
optionC: Specify both test classes and individual test methods that are required to be executed, as both are supported in DeployOptions.
optionD: To run a subset of tests, set the RunLocalTests test level on the DeployOptions object and pass it as an argument to the deploy() call.
explanation:
Specifying test methods not being supported in DeployOptions, so only test classes are specified, and setting the Run Specified Tests test level on DeployOptions and passing it to deploy(), are the two true statements. Salesforce has a page written for exactly this task, and it settles the granularity in one sentence: "You can specify only test classes. You can't specify individual test methods." Its example passes an array of class names - {"TestClass1", "TestClass2", "TestClass3"} - to setRunTests. The reference documentation agrees: runTests is "a list of Apex tests to run during deployment. Specify the class name, one name per instance", and the Salesforce CLI behaves the same way, with --tests taking test class names.
So both keyed statements are true. Method-level selection is not available, which is precisely why you specify the classes that cover the components being deployed; and the mechanism for running that subset is to set the RunSpecifiedTests test level on DeployOptions and pass it to the deploy() call, at which point "only the tests that you specify in the runTests option are run".
One constraint to plan around when you narrow the test set: "if the code coverage of an Apex component in the deployment is less than 75%, the deployment fails". Choosing too few classes does not just weaken the safety net, it can block the deployment outright.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Both classes and individual methods are supported) — contradicts the documentation directly; only class names are accepted.
Option D (RunLocalTests as the subset level) — not a subset in any useful sense; it runs "all tests in your org... except the ones that originate from installed managed and unlocked packages", which on a mature org is most of the suite.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy_run_specific_tests.htm

corrected.note: Answer moved B,C to A,B, and option A was repaired. The scrape had dropped a negation from option A, turning "Specifying the test method is not supported in DeployOptions" into its opposite and leaving a self-contradictory sentence; restoring it makes A true and the item answerable. Salesforce's Running a Subset of Tests in a Deployment states "You can specify only test classes. You can't specify individual test methods", so the previously keyed option asserting method-level support is false.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is using Salesforce for their sales organization. The sales users have created several dashboards using multiple running users. The admins have also added a few workflow rules that send email notifications to some sales users. What should an Architect consider while planning the deployment of such components? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: If the username in the source org doesn't exist in the target org, the deployment will stop until the usernames are resolved or removed.
optionB: User fields are preserved during metadata deployments and Salesforce attempts to locate a matching user in the target org during deployment.
optionC: If the username in the source org doesn't exist in the target org, the deployment will continue and Salesforce will automatically create the username in the target org.
optionD: User fields are ignored during metadata deployments and all such users need to be manually created in the target org before starting the deployment.
explanation:
The deployment stopping until a missing username is resolved or removed, and user fields being preserved with Salesforce attempting to locate a matching user in the target org, are the two considerations. User references really do travel inside the component XML rather than being stripped out - a dashboard's runningUser field holds "the username of the user whose role and sharing settings are used to determine the data shown in the dashboard", and workflow email alerts carry their recipients the same way. On deployment Salesforce resolves those usernames against the target org, which is why the usual advice is to make sure the referenced users exist there first.
The dashboard case has a documented fallback that is worth knowing, because it fails quietly rather than loudly: "when you deploy a dashboard and the value in this field is not defined or does not correspond to a valid user, the field is populated with the username of the user performing the deployment". The deployment succeeds and the dashboard now runs as whoever deployed it - which can show every user data they should not see. Check running users after a deployment rather than trusting that a clean result means they came across intact.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Salesforce automatically creates the missing username) — Salesforce never creates a user as part of a deployment.
Option D (User fields are ignored and users must be created manually first) — the fields are not discarded; they travel in the XML and are resolved against the target org.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_dashboard.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands, but the old explanation was wrong about dashboards specifically. It said a missing username stops the deployment until it is resolved; the Metadata API documents the opposite for a dashboard runningUser - the field is silently populated with the username of the user performing the deployment, so the deployment succeeds with the wrong running user.

question: Universal Containers has a highly customized Salesforce org, with many different pieces of configuration and code. Which configuration item should be covered by executable tests?
optionA: Workflow Rules
optionB: Case Assignment Rules
optionC: Active Process Builders
optionD: Validation Rules
explanation:
Validation Rules are the configuration item to cover with executable tests, and they are the cleanest of these to cover. They fire on every insert and update as part of the standard save order, so a test method can attempt a save with invalid data, catch the DmlException, and assert on the message - the rule's logic is verified directly, with no configuration needed to provoke it.
The comparison is a matter of difficulty, not possibility, and that is where the old reasoning went wrong. Workflow rules and processes also execute during the save order in a test, and their field updates can be asserted by requerying the record afterwards. Case assignment rules are the genuine outlier: Apex controls them explicitly through Database.DMLOptions, where setting assignmentRuleHeader.useDefaultRule tells the system to "use the default (active) assignment rule for the case or lead" - so a test that simply inserts a Case is not exercising the rule at all unless it sets that option.
Currency note: two of the options name automation Salesforce has moved on from. Workflow Rules and Process Builder reached end of support at the end of 2025, with Flow as the replacement, so new automation being written for test coverage today would be Flow rather than either of them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Workflow Rules) — testable, since they run in the save order, but only indirectly by requerying for their field updates, and the automation is now end-of-support.
Option B (Case Assignment Rules) — not exercised by a plain insert; a test must set DMLOptions.assignmentRuleHeader for the rule to fire at all.
Option C (Active Process Builders) — the same indirect coverage as workflow rules, on automation that is also end-of-support.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_class_Database_AssignmentRuleHeader.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_code_coverage_intro.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation claimed the behaviour of workflow rules and processes "cannot be directly asserted" in unit tests. They do execute during the save order in a test and their effects can be asserted; the option that genuinely does not run unless Apex asks for it is the assignment rule, via Database.DMLOptions.assignmentRuleHeader.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing Salesforce and wants the custom code to be unit-tested for all adverse conditions. Which two best practices should an Architect recommend while implementing Test Classes? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Test classes should not create custom setting data.
optionB: Test classes must use existing data in the environment.
optionC: Execute test classes under various profiles.
optionD: Test data must have positive as well as negative data.
explanation:
Executing test classes under various profiles, and test data with positive as well as negative data, are the two best practices. Testing for adverse conditions means two things here. Data has to include the values that should fail - nulls, boundary values, oversized inputs, bulk volumes - because a suite built only from valid records proves the happy path and nothing else. And the tests have to run as more than one kind of user: much of what breaks in an enterprise org breaks because of who is running the code, so exercising the logic under different profiles and permission sets is what catches missing object and field access before a user finds it.
One detail worth having right when you use System.runAs for this: the documentation now states that a runAs block enforces the user's sharing rules and their object-level and field-level permissions, regardless of the sharing mode of the test class. The older understanding that runAs affects record sharing only is out of date.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Test classes should not create custom setting data) — the opposite of convention; a test creates whatever the code under test reads, including custom setting values.
Option B (Tests must use existing environment data) — tests do not see org data by default; isolation is the default behaviour, which is precisely why a test creates the records it needs.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_code_coverage_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_load_data.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is planning to move to Salesforce Sales Cloud and retire its homegrown on-premise system. As part of the project, UC will need to migrate 5 million Accounts, 10 million Contacts, and 5 million Leads to Salesforce. Which three areas should be tested as part of data migration? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Account and Lead ownership
optionB: Contact association with correct Account
optionC: Page layout assignments
optionD: Lead assignment
explanation:
Account and Lead ownership, Contact association with the correct Account, and data transformation against the source system are the three areas to test. Record ownership must be verified to ensure every Account and Lead is assigned to the correct Salesforce user post-migration - ownership errors break visibility, sharing and assignment rules. Contact-to-Account relationships are the most critical structural integrity check in an Account and Contact migration; mis-linked or orphaned Contacts break the data model. And data transformation validation - comparing migrated field values against the source system - confirms all mappings, format conversions and transformation rules executed correctly.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Page layout assignments) — metadata configuration, not migration data.
Option D (Lead assignment) — rule configuration, not a data integrity concern for the migration itself.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has been on the org development model with scratch orgs already enabled, but they haven't been taking advantage of scratch orgs. Now UC is ready to move to the package development model. What step must be done by an administrator?
optionA: In setup, switch the Enable Unlocked Packages to Enabled, keep the Enable Second-Generation Managed Packages as disabled.
optionB: In setup, switch the Enable Dev Hub to Enabled, then switch the Enable Source Tracking for Scratch Orgs to Enabled.
optionC: In setup, switch the Enable Unlocked Packages and Second-Generation Managed Packages to Enabled.
optionD: In setup, switch both the Enable Dev Hub and Enable 2nd-Generation Managed Packages to Enabled.
explanation:
Switching Enable Unlocked Packages and Second-Generation Managed Packages to Enabled in Setup is the step. Scratch orgs are a Dev Hub feature, so an org already using them has Dev Hub enabled - that prerequisite is met and re-enabling it is not the missing step. What remains is a single toggle. The Salesforce DX Developer Guide gives the path: from Setup, enter Dev Hub in the Quick Find box, select Dev Hub, and select "Enable Unlocked Packages and Second-Generation Managed Packages". One setting gates both package types, which is why no option that turns on only one of them describes a real Setup screen.
Worth knowing before you flip it: "After you enable this setting, you can't disable it."
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Enable Unlocked Packages only, keep 2GP disabled) — no such split exists; one setting gates both package types.
Option B (Enable Dev Hub, then Enable Source Tracking for Scratch Orgs) — Dev Hub is already on, since scratch orgs are in use, and source tracking is not the packaging gate.
Option D (Enable Dev Hub and Enable 2nd-Generation Managed Packages) — Dev Hub is already enabled, and the packaging toggle is the combined setting, not a 2GP-only one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_setup_enable_secondgen_pkg.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm

question: Sales and Service products will be created by two teams using 2nd-generation managed packages. The Sales team needs to use a specific function of the Service product, but only the functions exposed by the Service team. No other team will use these functions. What should an architect recommend?
optionA: Create two 2GP packages with the same namespace; set the methods to be shared with @namespaceAccessible.
optionB: Create two managed packages with Sales and Service namespaces; set the methods with @salesAccessible.
optionC: Create two managed packages, one for each product.
optionD: Create a single 2GP with one namespace exposing all methods.
explanation:
Two 2GP packages with the same namespace, with the shared methods marked @namespaceAccessible, is the recommendation. The requirement is selective exposure between two packages owned by the same company, and Salesforce provides one annotation for exactly that. @NamespaceAccessible makes "public Apex in a package available to other packages that use the same namespace", applying to classes, methods, interfaces, properties and abstract classes in a second-generation package. Without it, public Apex in a 2GP package is not reachable from another package at all.
So the Service team builds its package in the shared namespace and annotates only the methods the Sales team is meant to call; everything else stays invisible. Note the escape hatch the annotation exists to avoid - global Apex is "always available across all namespaces, and needs no annotation", which would expose the functions to anyone, not just the Sales package.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Separate Sales and Service namespaces with @salesAccessible) — two packages in different namespaces have no such channel, and the annotation named after one of the products does not exist.
Option C (Two managed packages, one per product) — with no shared namespace and no annotation there is no way to expose the Service functions selectively.
Option D (A single 2GP exposing all methods) — throws away the separation the two teams need.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_NamespaceAccessible.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: What are three advantages of the package development model? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Eliminating the need of using change sets, which should no longer be used.
optionB: Providing its own source control.
optionC: Improving team development and collaboration.
optionD: Facilitating automated testing and continuous integration.
optionE: Significantly reducing the need for manually tracking changes.
explanation:
Improving team development and collaboration, facilitating automated testing and continuous integration, and significantly reducing the need to manually track changes are the three advantages. Packages have clear ownership and versioning that improve collaboration between teams; package-based development integrates naturally with CI/CD pipelines, since packages can be automatically built, versioned and installed; and package versions replace manual change tracking because the version history is the audit trail.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Eliminates change sets, which should no longer be used) — the model does not eliminate change sets entirely; many orgs still rely on them.
Option B (Provides its own source control) — packages do not provide source control; Git or another VCS is still required separately.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm

question: All AppExchange products are subject to Salesforce security reviews. What is the most common reason AppExchange products fail the security review?
optionA: SOQL injection
optionB: Cross-site scripting
optionC: CRUD/FLS (field-level security)
optionD: Session hacking
explanation:
CRUD/FLS (field-level security) enforcement is the most common reason. Salesforce publishes the ranking, and it is not close. Its review of AppExchange submissions states that "object and field level security (CRUD/FLS) enforcement vulnerabilities are the top reason (by a significant margin) for failing the AppExchange security review" - code that queries or writes without first checking whether the running user may see or change the object and fields involved. The reason it dominates is structural: a packaged class runs in orgs whose permission configurations the developer has never seen, so anything that assumes access is a finding by default.
Currency note on the remedy: the modern way to satisfy this is to run queries and DML in user mode rather than hand-writing permission checks, with Security.stripInaccessible available to remove fields the running user cannot access from results.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SOQL injection) — a real finding, but number ten in Salesforce's published list.
Option B (Cross-site scripting) — also real, at number eight in the same list.
Option D (Session hacking) — not among the leading causes Salesforce reports.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2023/08/the-top-20-vulnerabilities-found-in-the-appexchange-security-review
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.packagingGuide.meta/packagingGuide/security_review_guidelines.htm

question: Universal Containers has multiple development teams working on separate streams with different timelines. Each stream has different releases and delivery dates. What is a suitable branching policy to recommend?
optionA: GitHub flow
optionB: Trunk-based development
optionC: Scratch-org-based development
optionD: Leaf-based development
explanation:
GitHub flow is the suitable branching policy. The requirement is that streams with different release dates do not block each other, so the branching model has to let work live apart from the mainline until its own release is ready. GitHub flow does that: each stream develops on its own branch, is reviewed through a pull request, and merges on its own schedule.
One caveat for real use: teams with genuinely staggered release dates often adopt a model with explicit release branches, which is a closer fit than either option here. This item's option set does not offer one, so the feature-branch model is the best available answer rather than the whole answer.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Trunk-based development) — assumes the opposite: very short-lived branches integrated into a single trunk continuously, which works when everyone releases together and fights the requirement when they do not.
Option C (Scratch-org-based development) — describes how environments are provisioned, not how branches are organized.
Option D (Leaf-based development) — not a branching model at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses Salesforce Performance Edition and is hosting weekly training sessions for 4 weeks (5 days each, new trainees weekly). UC wants to train on samples of production data and delete data at week-end. What is the optimal recommendation?
optionA: Refresh a Partial Copy sandbox every weekend and include an appropriate sandbox template.
optionB: Refresh a Developer Pro sandbox every weekend and include an appropriate sandbox template.
optionC: Refresh a Partial Copy sandbox every weekend and load data needed using Data Loader.
optionD: Refresh a Developer Pro sandbox every weekend and load data needed using Data Loader.
explanation:
Refreshing a Partial Copy sandbox every weekend with an appropriate sandbox template is the optimal recommendation. Two documented facts decide this. First, "sandbox templates are only available for use with Full or Partial Copy sandboxes" - so pairing a template with a Developer Pro sandbox describes something the platform will not do. Second, Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes copy metadata only; no production records arrive in them at all, whatever their storage allocation, so any option built on one ends in a manual Data Loader run every single week.
The Partial Copy refresh with a template seeds a representative sample of production data automatically on each refresh - up to 10,000 records per selected object. Its 5-day refresh interval comfortably supports a weekend refresh between cohorts, and the refresh itself wipes the previous week's work, which is the requirement to delete the data at week end.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Developer Pro with a sandbox template) — templates are only available for Full or Partial Copy sandboxes, so this is not something the platform will do.
Option C (Partial Copy plus Data Loader) — the template already seeds the sample; a manual load every week is the work the template removes.
Option D (Developer Pro plus Data Loader) — no production data arrives in a Developer Pro sandbox, so every week ends in a manual load.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.data_sandbox_templates.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000381868&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers uses the org development model and Salesforce CLI. A feature release artifact (.zip file) has been tested in a lower sandbox and is being deployed to a full sandbox for performance testing. Quick deployment options are NOT being used. What is the correct deployment approach?
optionA: Authorize to Full sandbox; Validate with sfdx:source:deploy; Deploy with sfdx:source:deploy.
optionB: Authorize to Full sandbox; Validate with sfdx:mdapi:deploy; Deploy with sfdx:source:deploy.
optionC: Authorize to Full sandbox; Validate with sfdx:mdapi:deploy; Deploy with sfdx:mdapi:deploy.
optionD: Authorize to Full sandbox; Validate with sfdx:source:deploy; Deploy with sfdx:mdapi:deploy.
explanation:
Validating with sfdx:mdapi:deploy and deploying with sfdx:mdapi:deploy is the correct approach, because the artefact decides the command. A .zip is Metadata API format - the package.xml-and-components layout that deploy() consumes - while the source-format commands expect an unpacked Salesforce DX project directory. Since the same artefact is being validated and then deployed, both steps have to use the Metadata API form of the command; pairing one of each fails at whichever step is handed a layout it cannot read.
Currency note: these sfdx-style commands belong to the previous CLI generation. The current equivalents are sf project deploy validate and sf project deploy start, which accept a Metadata API format directory or zip through a dedicated flag. The reasoning the question tests is unchanged - match the command family to the artefact format - but the command names have moved on.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (source:deploy for both) — the source commands expect a DX project directory, not a .zip.
Option B (mdapi validate, source deploy) — the deploy step is handed a layout it cannot read.
Option D (source validate, mdapi deploy) — the validate step fails for the same reason.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_validate.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has 80% code coverage. Despite having a test plan for each sprint, the number of defects is large. What two items should the architect recommend to reduce defects? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The test script should be used to define the test classes.
optionB: The code coverage should be increased to 95%.
optionC: The test analyst who creates the test plan must also create the test classes.
optionD: The acceptance criteria should have more details.
explanation:
Using the test script to define the test classes, and giving the acceptance criteria more detail, are the two recommendations. Coverage is already above the platform's requirement, so it is not what is letting the defects through. Salesforce says as much: unit tests "must cover at least 75% of your Apex code, and those tests must pass", but "code coverage serves as one indication of test effectiveness, but doesn't guarantee test effectiveness. The quality of the tests also matters".
The two keyed answers attack the real gaps. Deriving test classes from the test scripts makes the automated tests exercise the scenarios the business actually described, including the edge cases a coverage-driven test never reaches. Sharper acceptance criteria shrink the gap the defects are escaping through - much of what is being logged as a defect is a difference of interpretation between what was specified and what was built.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Increase code coverage to 95%) — buys more executed lines, not more assertions about behaviour anyone cares about.
Option C (The test analyst also writes the test classes) — removes the independent second reading, which is the point of having both.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_code_coverage_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers' architect is documenting the Application Lifecycle Management (ALM) process to communicate it to development teams from different implementation partners. Which three steps apply to any Salesforce development project? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Environment management
optionB: Test or validation
optionC: Continuous integration
optionD: Build release
explanation:
Environment management, test or validation, and build release are the three steps that apply to any Salesforce development project. The question asks which steps apply to any project, so the answer has to be tool-agnostic. Every project needs somewhere to build and test, needs its changes verified before promotion, and needs the changes gathered into something deployable. Salesforce's current framing of the lifecycle is the same shape - plan, build, test, deploy, monitor.
Currency note: the classic Salesforce Development Lifecycle Guide that this vocabulary comes from has been retired, and the lifecycle is now described through the five phases above and through DevOps Center.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Continuous integration) — a practice a team may or may not adopt within those steps, not a step every project performs.
Option E (Change sets) — one deployment tool among several; a project using the Metadata API or packages performs the same release step without them.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.deploy_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has two full sandboxes — 'Stage' for performance/regression testing and another for UAT. Both were refreshed two months ago. UC is targeting UAT completion in two weeks and a production release in four weeks. A Salesforce major release is scheduled in six weeks. UC needs to release on the current Salesforce version. What should the architect recommend?
optionA: Refresh both sandboxes immediately to get the preview release and complete testing.
optionB: Proceed with the current sandbox versions and release before the Salesforce upgrade.
optionC: Refresh only the UAT sandbox and keep Stage on the current version.
optionD: Delay the release until after the Salesforce major release.
explanation:
Proceeding with the current sandbox versions and releasing before the Salesforce upgrade is the recommendation. The release lands four weeks out and the platform upgrade six weeks out, so production is still on the current version on go-live day and the existing sandboxes already match it. Testing that has been running for two months against that version stays valid.
Refreshing now is what would break it. During the transition between major releases Salesforce creates preview sandboxes by default, so a refresh in this window puts the sandbox on the next release and every completed test has to be re-run against a platform version production will not be on at go-live. A Full sandbox also cannot be refreshed more often than every 29 days, so that decision could not be undone before the release.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Refresh both sandboxes now for the preview release) — puts both on the next release, invalidating two months of testing against a version production will not be on at go-live, and the 29-day limit means it cannot be undone in time.
Option C (Refresh only UAT, keep Stage current) — splits the train across two platform versions, and UAT would then be accepting on a release production will not have.
Option D (Delay until after the major release) — gives up the current-version window the business asked for.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) operates globally with regional production orgs for Americas, EMEA, and APAC due to regulatory requirements. Each org has regional customizations AND shared standard features. How should shared metadata be deployed across all regional production orgs?
optionA: Deploy metadata to production orgs using managed packages.
optionB: Deploy metadata to production orgs using unmanaged packages.
optionC: Deploy metadata to production orgs using the package development model.
optionD: Deploy metadata to production orgs using change sets.
explanation:
Deploying the shared metadata to the production orgs using managed packages is the answer. Three independent production orgs have no deployment connection between them, so change sets cannot reach across them at all - a change set travels between a production org and its own sandboxes. That leaves a package, and the choice is about what happens after installation. A managed package is versioned and upgradeable, so the shared standard features can be pushed forward centrally release after release while each region keeps its own local customizations around them.
Worth knowing when you make this call for real: Salesforce positions unlocked packages as the right type "for most use cases" when you are not distributing on AppExchange, and they are versioned and upgradeable in the same way. This option set does not offer them, but for internal multi-org distribution they are the modern equivalent of the answer here rather than a lesser one.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Unmanaged packages) — installs once and is then just ordinary metadata in each org, with no upgrade path; the three orgs would diverge from the first regional edit onward.
Option C (The package development model) — a way of working, not a deployment vehicle; it says nothing about which package type carries the shared features into three orgs.
Option D (Change sets) — travel only between a production org and its own sandboxes, so they cannot reach across independent regional orgs.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.packagingGuide.meta/packagingGuide/packaging_developing_unmanaged.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has multi-cloud architecture in a single org. The Sales Cloud dev team is working in a Dev Pro sandbox (DevPro1) delivering a release in three months. The business requirements from Service Cloud warrant a quicker release in four weeks, but need part of the Sales Cloud work that is completed in DevPro1. The decision of using a separate Dev Pro sandbox (DevPro2) is still pending. DevPro1 was upgraded to preview for the next Salesforce major release two weeks ago. What should an Architect recommend?
optionA: Clone the DevPro1 sandbox and name it DevPro2 for the second work stream to work on the Service Cloud requirements.
optionB: Push back on the requirements because adding another work stream will bring some risks with it.
optionC: Ask the second work stream team to work on the same DevPro1 sandbox.
optionD: DevPro1 cannot be cloned because it is on a different version from Production. Just create a new DevPro2, and migrate metadata from DevPro1.
explanation:
Cloning the DevPro1 sandbox as DevPro2 for the Service Cloud work stream is the recommendation. The premise of the option that rules cloning out has been false since Spring '20: Salesforce supports cloning a sandbox whose release version differs from production, which is exactly the case for a DevPro1 already upgraded to the preview release. So the restriction that option invokes no longer exists, and cloning is available.
Cloning is also what the scenario needs. A clone of DevPro1 hands the Service Cloud stream an environment that already contains the completed Sales Cloud work, with no metadata migration to build and no chance of missing a dependency.
One caveat to plan around: a cross-version clone "may take significantly longer than a standard sandbox refresh, especially during sandbox preview release months", it can run for hours or days with no service level agreement, and Salesforce suggests a brand-new sandbox as the faster route when time is tight. With four weeks to deliver, start the clone immediately and keep that fallback in view.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Push back on the requirements) — not an architectural option; the business need is real and the platform supports meeting it.
Option C (Second stream works in DevPro1) — two teams changing one org while a three-month release is in flight.
Option D (DevPro1 cannot be cloned across versions, so build DevPro2 and migrate) — a false premise; cross-version cloning has been supported since Spring '20, and a manual metadata migration risks missing a dependency the clone would carry.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000380490&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: UC's scale of Salesforce deployment has increased over time, leading to complexities. UC is finding too many bugs in the deployed code, which has become a challenge to the delivery team. The team wants to reduce the amount of bugs by ensuring all the developed code is reviewed, tested, and validated in the upstream deployment process. Which three development practices will be best suited to address UC's concerns? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Use continuous integration with automation testing.
optionB: Encourage the development team to be self-organizing.
optionC: Enable developer teams to do peer code review.
optionD: Incorporate test-driven deployment into the project structure.
optionE: Enable a short and timely feedback loop with customers.
explanation:
Continuous integration with automation testing, peer code review, and test-driven deployment are the three practices best suited to UC's concerns - the three upstream quality gates that directly address reviewing, testing and validating code before it reaches production. CI with automated testing means every commit triggers a test run that catches defects immediately; a required peer review step ensures every change is inspected before merging; and test-driven practice, writing the tests first, ensures all code is validated by design.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Self-organizing development teams) — an Agile structure concept, not a quality gate.
Option E (Short feedback loop with customers) — operates downstream, after deployment, so it does not address upstream validation.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html

question: What are three advantages of using the SFDX? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Can store code on a local machine, or a version control system.
optionB: Can quickly deploy metadata using Execute Anonymous.
optionC: Can create scratch orgs.
optionD: Can use native Deployment Rollback Tool to quickly revert to prior state.
optionE: Can install application metadata from a central repository.
explanation:
Storing code on a local machine or in a version control system, creating scratch orgs, and installing application metadata from a central repository are the three advantages - the shape of Salesforce DX itself. Source lives on the developer's machine and in version control rather than only inside an org, which is the shift the whole model rests on. Scratch orgs are available on demand - "a source-driven and disposable deployment of Salesforce code and metadata" - so an environment can be created per feature branch or per CI run. And package versions can be installed into any org from Salesforce's own package registry, which is how the same artefact reaches each environment.
Naming note: the commands have moved from the sfdx force: form to the current sf ones, so package installation today is sf package install rather than the older syntax.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Deploy metadata using Execute Anonymous) — Execute Anonymous runs a block of Apex in an org; it deploys no metadata.
Option D (Native Deployment Rollback Tool) — there is no native rollback command in the CLI; reversing a deployment means deploying the previous state and removing new components with a destructiveChanges manifest.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html

question: Which are two key benefits of fully integrating an agile issue tracker with software testing and continuous integration tools? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Developers can see automated test statuses post code commit on a specific user story.
optionB: Developers can collaborate and communicate effectively on specific user stories.
optionC: Developers can observe their team velocity on the burn chart report in the agile tool.
optionD: Developers can use the committed code's build status directly on the user story record.
explanation:
Seeing automated test statuses post-commit on a specific user story, and using the committed code's build status directly on the user story record, are the two key benefits. The benefit of wiring the tracker to the build pipeline is that the story record becomes the place where the state of its code is visible. A commit tied to a story triggers the pipeline, and both the automated test results and the build status come back to that story - so a developer, or anyone reading the board, can see whether the work is green without opening the CI tool and matching commits to stories by hand.
The two rejected benefits are things the tracker already does on its own.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Collaborate and communicate on user stories) — available in any issue tracker, integrated or not.
Option C (Observe team velocity on the burn chart) — drawn from the tracker's own estimates and status transitions; it does not improve when CI is connected.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers business users often observe that newly released features are resulting in other previously existing and stable functionality being broken. Which approach should an Architect recommend to prevent regression?
optionA: Utilize the developer console to run test suites for the affected functionality.
optionB: Utilize unit and functional test automation as part of a continuous integration strategy.
optionC: Utilize Salesforce Apex Hammer to automatically test all functionality.
optionD: Freeze development of new features and re-architect the system to remove the bugs.
explanation:
Unit and functional test automation as part of a continuous integration strategy is the approach. Regression is a timing problem: the break is introduced during development and discovered by users after release. Only automated tests running on every commit close that gap - the suite runs against each change, and a failure names the commit that caused it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Run test suites from the Developer Console) — the same tests without the trigger, so it depends on someone remembering, at the moment it matters, on every release.
Option C (Salesforce Apex Hammer) — Salesforce's own process for validating that a platform release does not break customer tests; it runs on Salesforce's side, and no customer can invoke it as a regression suite.
Option D (Freeze development and re-architect) — addresses the existing defects while guaranteeing the next release reintroduces the problem, because nothing has changed about how regressions are caught.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_code_coverage_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) deploys major releases on a monthly schedule. In recent months, the team has noticed the deployment time has increased two-fold from 2 hours to 4 hours. The team wants to get back to reasonable deployment times. Which three issues could be affecting their deployment times? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: The number and complexity of Apex tests will have a large impact on the deployment time.
optionB: Some components — profiles, custom junction objects, and fields — take longer to process than others.
optionC: The deployments are being scheduled during off-peak hours, which is not the best time.
optionD: Users are working in the org during deployment — locking can affect users and the deployment.
optionE: The team is highly constrained with pre-deployment and post-deployment changes.
explanation:
The number and complexity of Apex tests, components such as profiles, junction objects and fields taking longer to process, and users working in the org during the deployment are the three issues that could be affecting deployment time. Apex tests are the largest single variable in a deployment window, because the platform runs them as part of the deploy and their cost grows with the suite. Component type matters too: Salesforce notes that "changes made to sharing rules or group settings, or structural changes in role hierarchy, can cause Apex code to recompile", and that deploying profile or permission set changes alongside sharing rules "triggers a calculation each time you attempt to deploy, which can be time-consuming if there are multiple failures". And an org full of working users is a slower target - record and metadata contention during the deploy is exactly why the guidance is to release "at times when most users are off the system".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Deployments scheduled during off-peak hours) — deploying off-peak is the recommendation, not a cause of slowness.
Option E (Constraints on pre- and post-deployment changes) — shape the process, not the platform's processing time.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

question: What are two things needed to delete metadata with a deploy() call? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Package.xml file.
optionB: The current API version must be used.
optionC: DestructiveChanges.xml file.
optionD: PurgeOnDelete option must be set to TRUE.
explanation:
A package.xml file and a destructiveChanges.xml file are the two things needed. A destructive deployment is an ordinary deploy with one extra manifest. Salesforce documents it directly: "to delete components, use the same procedure as with deploying components, but also include a delete manifest file that's named destructiveChanges.xml and list the components to delete in this manifest". The ordinary manifest still has to be there - package.xml must "list no components to deploy, include the API version, and be in the same directory as destructiveChanges.xml".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (The current API version must be used) — the API version in package.xml simply has to be one the platform still supports, not the newest.
Option D (purgeOnDelete set to true) — optional: "to bypass the Recycle Bin, set the purgeOnDelete option to true", which changes where the deleted components go, not whether the call works.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy_deleting_files.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

question: A Salesforce contractor has built an application for Universal Containers (UC). The contractor will need to deploy multiple times from the contractor's own Salesforce to UC's Salesforce environments. Ultimately, UC has full control of the application's code, including its intellectual property. Which deployment method should the contractor use?
optionA: Eclipse IDE.
optionB: Unmanaged Package.
optionC: Change Sets.
optionD: Managed Package.
explanation:
An unmanaged package is the deployment method. Two requirements decide it: the contractor deploys repeatedly from their own org into the customer's, and the customer ends up owning the code outright. An unmanaged package does both - it is documented as the vehicle for "a one-time drop of applications that require customization after installation", and once installed its components are ordinary metadata that UC can read, edit and extend.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Eclipse IDE) — edits and deploys but packages nothing for repeated installation.
Option C (Change Sets) — cannot cross two unrelated orgs, since they require a deployment connection between a production org and its own sandboxes.
Option D (Managed Package) — built for the opposite outcome: the format "used by Salesforce partners to distribute and sell applications to customers", it locks its components against modification in the subscriber org and keeps control with the publisher, which is precisely the arrangement UC does not want.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.packagingGuide.meta/packagingGuide/packaging_developing_unmanaged.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pkg1_dev.meta/pkg1_dev/sharing_apps.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which two options should be considered when making production changes in a highly regulated and audited environment? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: All changes including hotfixes should be reviewed against security principles.
optionB: Any production change should have explicit stakeholder approval.
optionC: No manual steps should be carried out.
optionD: After deployment, the development team should test and verify functionality in production.
explanation:
Reviewing all changes including hotfixes against security principles, and requiring explicit stakeholder approval for any production change, are the two considerations. Regulation and audit turn every production change into something that has to be justified afterwards, so the two answers are both about evidence. Reviewing every change against security principles has to include hotfixes, because the emergency path is where controls are most often skipped and where an auditor will look first. Explicit stakeholder approval is what produces the record that the change was authorized, by someone entitled to authorize it, before it happened.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (No manual steps at all) — an admirable target but not a requirement; a documented, approved manual step is auditable, and some post-deployment configuration cannot be automated.
Option D (Development team tests in production after deployment) — the wrong order: validation belongs in a pre-production environment, and a regulated change that has to be tested in production has been released before it was proven.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) is working on a major project and has determined that its approach to a certain feature will no longer work with an upcoming Salesforce platform release (e.g., Winter to Spring). What should a Technical Architect recommend to address this issue?
optionA: Continue with the current approach, since Salesforce will rectify the issue prior to updating the production environment to the new platform release.
optionB: Continue development in a non-upgraded sandbox, and have the developer update the API version of the code to the upcoming API version for testing purposes.
optionC: Submit a request to Salesforce to enable the 'delay upgrade' feature in their org. Have the UC administrator schedule the upgrade for a later date.
optionD: Determine the developer sandbox upgrade schedule, and have the developer refactor the approach to the feature in the upgraded sandbox.
explanation:
Determining the developer sandbox upgrade schedule and having the developer refactor the feature in the upgraded sandbox is the recommendation. The platform upgrade arrives on Salesforce's schedule, so the only useful move is to meet the new release early in an environment that already has it. That is precisely what sandbox preview is for: a preview sandbox "provides early access to new features and lets you test your configurations before the production upgrade". Find which sandboxes are on preview instances, take the affected feature there, and refactor it while production is still on the current release.
The alternatives all avoid the work rather than doing it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Continue; Salesforce will rectify it before production upgrades) — waiting for Salesforce to accommodate custom code that a documented change breaks is not a strategy the customer controls.
Option B (Stay in a non-upgraded sandbox and raise the code's API version) — raising the API version of a class does not put the runtime on the new release, so it tests nothing about the actual behaviour change.
Option C (Request a 'delay upgrade' feature and schedule it later) — deferring a major release to a date of the org's choosing is not something a customer can request.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is looking to install a new application to enable advanced quoting in its current Professional Edition org. The org is near capacity with object and tab limits. Which two solutions should the Architect recommend? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Install an Aloha certified App.
optionB: Upgrade to an Enterprise Edition org.
optionC: Create and install an unmanaged package.
optionD: Buy more user licenses to increase org limits.
explanation:
Installing an Aloha certified app and upgrading to an Enterprise Edition org are the two solutions, and both relieve the constraint the way the documentation describes. A publicly posted AppExchange managed package is exempt from the subscriber org's allocations - "the custom objects that are contained in a managed package that's publicly posted on AppExchange don't count against the allocations for your Salesforce edition", and the same exemption covers Lightning apps, custom apps and custom tabs. Installing the quoting app as such a package therefore adds capability without consuming the capacity that is nearly gone. Upgrading the edition raises the ceiling itself: Professional Edition allows 50 custom objects, Enterprise Edition 200.
Two currency notes. "Aloha" is legacy vocabulary for this exemption; current documentation frames it as a managed package publicly posted on AppExchange, with no separate certification named. And the custom tab allocation is no longer the tight constraint the exam-era wording implies - Professional Edition is documented at 1,210 custom tabs and Enterprise at 1,225. Custom objects, at 50 against 200, are where the edition difference actually bites.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Create and install an unmanaged package) — the opposite trade: its components land as ordinary org metadata and count against every allocation.
Option D (Buy more user licenses) — licences buy seats, not schema, and do not move the object, tab or app allocations at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.overview_limits_professional.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.overview_limits_enterprise.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/isvforce/guide/dev-package-limits-for-pe-ge.html

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation taught stale allocations - Professional Edition at 10 custom tabs and Enterprise at 25. Current documentation puts them at 1,210 and 1,225; the real edition constraint is custom objects, 50 against 200.

question: A year has passed since a project has gone live and a developer is looking to make an update to an existing Apex class, but is unsure of its purpose. What artifact from the original project should be leveraged to determine the purpose of the class?
optionA: User Acceptance Test Scripts.
optionB: Test Execution Plan.
optionC: Requirements Traceability Matrix.
optionD: Test Sign Off Document.
explanation:
The Requirements Traceability Matrix is the artifact to leverage. The developer needs to know why the class exists, which is a requirements question rather than a testing one. A requirements traceability matrix is the artefact that carries that link: each requirement is mapped forward to the design elements and components that implement it and to the tests that verify it, so a class can be traced back to the business need that produced it a year ago.
Worth pairing with the practice that would have avoided the problem: the field and object description attributes are metadata and travel with the component, so intent recorded there stays attached to the thing it describes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (User Acceptance Test Scripts) — say what a tester did, not why the code was written.
Option B (Test Execution Plan) — says how and when tests were run.
Option D (Test Sign Off Document) — records that someone accepted the result; any of these may mention the feature by name, but none states the intent behind the class.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Why does Salesforce prohibit Stress Testing against Production?
optionA: There is not enough CPU.
optionB: It is a shared environment.
optionC: It is blocked by data center infrastructure.
optionD: It causes Internet congestion.
explanation:
Production being a shared environment is the reason. The reason is architectural rather than technical: production is shared infrastructure, so a test designed to drive one org to its breaking point degrades service for every other tenant on the same instance. Salesforce states the rule directly - "because Salesforce is a multitenant platform, performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox", and "scale tests are only permitted in sandboxes".
The prohibition comes with a process rather than a flat refusal. Testing in a sandbox needs prior approval, submitted "at least one week before the testing date" with a test plan, dates, the sandbox org id and the scenario, and "unapproved testing is subject to throttling or blocking".
The rejected options invent physical causes where the actual constraint is the obligation Salesforce has to its other customers on that instance.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Not enough CPU) — an invented physical cause; the constraint is the obligation to other tenants, not capacity.
Option C (Blocked by data center infrastructure) — nothing physically blocks it; unapproved testing is throttled or blocked as policy.
Option D (Causes Internet congestion) — likewise invented; the prohibition is about the shared instance, not the network.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a recruiting application using Metadata API version 35, deployed to production last year. The current Salesforce platform is running API version 36. A new field introduced on the object Apex page in API version 36 has been developed by a UC developer, who tries to deploy the page using the previous deployment script that uses API version 35. What will happen during the deployment?
optionA: The deployment script will pass because the new field is backward compatible with the previous API version 35.
optionB: The deployment script will fail because the new field is not known for the previous API version 35.
optionC: The deployment script will pass because the new field is supported on the current platform version.
optionD: The deployment script will fail because the platform does not support the previous API version 35.
explanation:
The deployment script will fail because the new field is not known for the previous API version 35. A deployment is validated against the API version declared in its manifest, not against whatever the platform happens to be running. A field introduced in the later version does not exist in the earlier version's schema, so a script pinned to the older version cannot describe it and the deployment fails on an unknown field. Raising the version in package.xml is the fix, and it is the only fix — the platform's own version does not rescue a manifest that claims an older one.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (passes, the field is backward compatible with version 35) — backward compatibility runs the other way: an older manifest can deploy older metadata, but it cannot describe a field that did not exist when that version shipped.
Option C (passes, the field is supported on the current platform version) — the platform supporting the field is not the question; the manifest's declared version is what the deployment is validated against.
Option D (fails because the platform does not support version 35) — a checkable claim, and false: Salesforce supports each API version "for a minimum of 3 years from the date of first release", and the retired band is 21.0 through 30.0 (retired Summer '25, after 7.0–20.0 went in Summer '22). Version 35.0 remains supported, which is exactly why the manifest version is where the failure comes from.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/api_rest_eol.htm
