question: The CTO at Universal Containers decided to implement the Scrum framework for its agile teams and communicated a set of Scrum principles to the company. Which describes a Scrum principle?
optionA: Deliver working software, so if a software component is working, avoid changing it.
optionB: Respect other teams by not doing their work (a developer should not test the software).
optionC: Create transparency by being honest and clear about timing, planning, and obstacles.
optionD: Embrace change by working on a different scope every day.
explanation:
Creating transparency by being honest and clear about timing, planning and obstacles is the Scrum principle. Transparency is foundational rather than incidental: teams are expected to be honest and clear about timing, progress, plans and obstacles, to speak up when help is needed, and to report back when an assumption turns out to be wrong. That visibility is what makes inspection possible, and inspection is what makes adaptation possible — each sprint's inspect-and-adapt point depends on the previous one having been reported truthfully.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (deliver working software, so avoid changing what works) — contradicts continuous improvement; Scrum expects the increment to keep evolving.
Option B (respect other teams by not doing their work, so a developer should not test) — contradicts the cross-functional team, where the team as a whole is accountable for a done increment.
Option D (embrace change by working on a different scope every day) — not embracing change: the sprint exists precisely so that change is absorbed between sprints rather than during them.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: Universal Containers (UC) has multiple teams with major projects working concurrently in their own developer sandboxes. After deploying to production, a bug is discovered. Due to tight timelines, the development team has suggested correcting the bug in the user acceptance testing (UAT) environment, which is a full copy sandbox. What should the architect recommend? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: UC should spin up a new sandbox to use as a hotfix environment and deploy the fix from there to production.
optionB: The fix should be made in the developer environment where the project work was done.
optionC: Since the issue was found in production, it should be treated as a change request and go through the change control process.
optionD: Correcting the bug in UAT is ideal since UAT is a full copy and will be the fastest.
explanation:
Spinning up a new sandbox as a hotfix environment and deploying the fix from there, and treating the production issue as a change request that goes through change control, are the two recommendations. Two things are wrong with fixing the bug in the UAT sandbox, and the keyed answers address one each. First, the environment: UAT is in use, and building an emergency fix there disturbs the testing other people are relying on while mixing the fix into whatever else that environment holds. A sandbox stood up as a hotfix environment isolates the change so that what reaches production is the fix and nothing else — Salesforce's environment-management guidance describes exactly this. Second, the governance: a defect discovered in production is a production change like any other. Tight timelines change how quickly change control runs, not whether it runs — the approval, the record of what was deployed and the rollback plan are what make the fix reversible if it makes things worse.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (fix it in the developer environment where the project work was done) — that sandbox holds in-flight project work, so the fix would arrive in production carrying whatever else that developer has built.
Option D (correcting the bug in UAT is ideal because it is a full copy and fastest) — measures only the first step, and ignores the contaminated test environment and the unapproved production change it leaves behind.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: There are many types of quality assurance techniques that can help minimize defects in software projects. Which two techniques should an architect recommend for Universal Containers to incorporate into its overall CI/CD pipeline? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Business verification testing.
optionB: Stress testing.
optionC: Automated browser testing.
optionD: Static code quality analysis.
explanation:
Automated browser testing and static code quality analysis are the two techniques to incorporate. A CI/CD pipeline can only include techniques that run unattended on every change, and both qualify. Static analysis runs at commit time against the source: Salesforce's own Code Analyzer unifies engines such as PMD, RetireJS and ESLint behind one CLI command, is designed to be integrated "into your build and deployment processes", and reports violations before the code has executed. Automated browser tests run after the deployment step and exercise the assembled application through the UI, which is the only layer that catches a break between components that each pass their own unit tests.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (business verification testing) — needs business users making judgments, which happens after a release reaches them; it cannot run unattended on every merge.
Option B (stress testing) — not permitted against production at all, and it needs advance approval even in a sandbox, so it cannot sit in a pipeline that runs on every change.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Salesforce has three major releases a year. Which type of change introduced by a release can cause automated browser tests to need updating?
optionA: DOM changes.
optionB: New standard fields.
optionC: Metadata schema changes.
optionD: New Apex methods.
explanation:
DOM changes are what break automated browser tests. Those tests — Selenium and WebDriver-based — navigate and assert on the rendered HTML Document Object Model, so when a Salesforce release changes the HTML structure, CSS class names or element IDs, the selectors in the tests no longer match and have to be updated.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (new standard fields) — a new field appears in the schema and on layouts where it is added; it does not alter the markup existing selectors target.
Option C (metadata schema changes) — affect deployments and API calls, not the rendered page structure a browser test asserts on.
Option D (new Apex methods) — server-side code, invisible to a test that drives the UI.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/lightning_testing_intro.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is using Sales and Service Cloud. They have two major releases and four minor releases every year, and maintain deployment (dev), integration, user acceptance (UAT), staging, and hotfix sandboxes. What should an Architect recommend when UC has P1 issues that must be fixed immediately?
optionA: Fix the issue in staging and deploy it into production.
optionB: Fix the issue in the hotfix sandbox, test, and deploy to production.
optionC: Fix the issue in development, test in UAT, and deploy to production.
optionD: Follow the release management process to move to production.
explanation:
Fixing the issue in the hotfix sandbox, testing, and deploying to production is what the architect should recommend. The organization has already built the answer: a hotfix sandbox is one of the environments it maintains, and it exists precisely so that a production emergency has a path that does not run through the release pipeline. Salesforce's environment-management guidance describes the same environment — a sandbox for urgent defects only — and the discipline that goes with it: fix, test, deploy, then merge the fix back into the in-flight release work so the next release does not undo it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (fix in staging and deploy) — staging holds the validated state of the next planned release, so deploying a fix from there ships that release early.
Option C (fix in development, test in UAT, deploy) — the full pipeline, correct for planned work and too slow for a P1.
Option D (follow the release management process) — the right answer to a different question: the point of a defined hotfix path is that emergencies are handled by an agreed exception rather than by suspending governance.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has an active production org and is planning to release new features next month. The team is preparing a deployment plan and reached out to the technical architect for inputs on the rollback strategy. What should a technical architect recommend?
optionA: Backup the existing metadata using the ANT Migration Tool. To roll back, deploy again to production using backed-up metadata.
optionB: Create a sandbox from production to take backup of existing metadata. To roll back, manually delete new components and redeploy using metadata from this sandbox.
optionC: Create a sandbox from production to take backup of existing metadata. To roll back, use destructiveChanges.xml to delete new components and redeploy original metadata from the sandbox.
optionD: Backup the existing metadata using the ANT Migration Tool. To roll back, manually delete new components and deploy again using backed-up metadata.
explanation:
Creating a sandbox from production to back up the existing metadata, then rolling back with a destructiveChanges.xml to delete the new components and redeploying the original metadata, is the recommendation. A rollback has two halves, and only one of them is a redeploy. Restoring the changed components is straightforward — deploy the pre-release metadata captured beforehand. Removing components the release added is not, because a deployment never deletes anything: the Metadata API only removes what a destructiveChanges.xml manifest names, alongside a package.xml that lists no components and carries the API version. Scripting that removal is what makes the rollback repeatable and reviewable. Taking the backup as a sandbox created from production gives a complete, self-consistent snapshot of the pre-deployment state, rather than a retrieval whose completeness depends on the manifest someone wrote at the time.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ANT backup, redeploy to roll back) — a redeploy restores changed components but deletes nothing, so every component the release added survives the rollback.
Option B (sandbox backup, manually delete then redeploy) — the right backup with the wrong removal: deleting components by hand in Setup is unrepeatable and easy to get wrong under pressure.
Option D (ANT backup, manually delete then redeploy) — both weaknesses at once — a retrieval-based backup and a manual deletion.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy_deleting_files.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing Service Cloud for their contact centers for 3,000 users and approximately 10 million customers. The average expected response time is less than 5 seconds with 1,500 concurrent users. What type of testing will help UC measure the page response time?
optionA: Unit testing.
optionB: Load testing.
optionC: System integration testing.
optionD: Stress testing.
explanation:
Load testing is what measures the page response time. The requirement is a response time at a stated concurrency — under 5 seconds with 1,500 concurrent users — which is the definition of a load test: drive the expected volume and measure what the system does at that volume.
Plan it in a Full sandbox sized like production, and submit the request before booking the window: "performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox", with tests approved in advance and unapproved testing "subject to throttling or blocking".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (unit testing) — establishes correctness at any scale; it produces no page response time.
Option C (system integration testing) — establishes that the systems exchange data correctly, not how fast a page renders under load.
Option D (stress testing) — the near miss: it deliberately exceeds the expected peak to find where the system fails, which answers a different question than "what is the response time at 1,500 users".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What three tools should an architect recommend to support application lifecycle management methodology? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Database management systems.
optionB: Version control repository.
optionC: Middleware.
optionD: Continuous integration tool.
explanation:
A version control repository, a continuous integration tool and an issue tracking tool are the three to recommend. They are the ones the lifecycle cannot run without: version control holds the source and its history, and is what makes the source rather than an org the record of what is being delivered; the CI tool executes the build, the tests and the deployment on every change instead of when someone remembers; and the issue tracker holds the work itself — the stories and defects the plan and build phases operate on — which is what connects a deployed change back to the request that caused it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (database management systems) — infrastructure that sits under an application; it does not participate in planning, building, testing or releasing a change.
Option C (middleware) — moves data between systems at run time, which is an integration concern rather than a lifecycle one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2

question: Universal Containers (UC) is preparing for the new Salesforce release in a couple of months and has several ongoing development projects that may be affected. Which three steps should the team at UC take to prepare for this release? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Contact Salesforce to schedule a time to upgrade the full sandbox.
optionB: Refresh a sandbox during the Release Preview Window to ensure they have the upcoming release.
optionC: Run regression tests in an upgraded sandbox to detect any issues with the upgrade.
optionD: Review the release notes for automatically-enabled features and technical debt.
optionE: Upgrade any SOAP integrations to the newest WSDL as early as possible.
explanation:
Refreshing a sandbox during the Release Preview Window, running regression tests in the upgraded sandbox, and reviewing the release notes are the three steps. They are the release-readiness loop. Refreshing inside the preview window puts a sandbox on an instance that takes the next release early — during that window Salesforce creates preview sandboxes by default — which gives the team a version of the platform production will not see for weeks. Regression testing there is what converts that access into information, and reading the release notes catches the features that switch themselves on and the behaviour changes no test was written for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (contact Salesforce to schedule the full sandbox upgrade) — upgrade timing is set by Salesforce and cannot be scheduled by the customer.
Option E (upgrade SOAP integrations to the newest WSDL) — a SOAP integration keeps working against the WSDL it was built on, since older API versions remain supported; regenerating it is work you do when you want something new, not release preparation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is building a new complex integration to a legacy system. The legacy system is also going through a major upgrade. Senior leadership has committed to the board that the combined programs will be completed on time. What is the risk with this plan?
optionA: The deadline is scheduled during a Salesforce release.
optionB: The project team has decided to use the Waterfall methodology.
optionC: The legacy system team is using an Agile methodology.
optionD: Multiple work-streams with dependencies could impact the go-live.
explanation:
Multiple work-streams with dependencies impacting the go-live is the risk. The integration is being built against a legacy system that is itself being upgraded, so the interface it targets is moving while it is being built — a slip or a design change on either side lands on the other, and the commitment made to the board covers both programmes as one date. Managing that coupling needs an explicit joint plan: agreed interface contracts, aligned milestones, and a shared view of what happens to the combined date if either side moves.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the deadline falls during a Salesforce release) — a scheduled, published event that can be planned around, and the preview window exists so a team can test against the new version in advance.
Option B (the team chose Waterfall) — a way of organising work, not a risk in itself.
Option C (the legacy team uses Agile) — the same: two teams can deliver on different methods provided the dependencies between them are managed.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is embarked on an enterprise Salesforce transformation journey. UC would like to streamline and automate deployment to different sandboxes during the build phase. Upon customer acceptance in UAT, the company also requested to automate the production deployment. As the deployment architect, what is the recommendation to satisfy the customer requirements?
optionA: Recommend using a Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment tool and build the pipeline to deploy to sandboxes and production.
optionB: Recommend using SFDX and document the deployment commands with steps to be executed for each environment.
optionC: Recommend using the ANT script and build a custom application to run the script and use change sets to deploy supported metadata.
optionD: Recommend using an AppExchange solution that packages deployment components and run the deployment wizard to track results.
explanation:
Using a Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment tool, with a pipeline built to deploy to sandboxes and production, is the recommendation. A CI/CD tool — Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps — automates builds, tests and deployments across every environment from developer sandboxes through to production, with the visibility and audit trail an enterprise transformation needs, and it is the only option that automates the production step the customer asked for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (SFDX with documented deployment commands) — the right underlying CLI, but documenting steps for a human to run is the manual process the requirement asks to remove.
Option C (ANT script plus a custom app and change sets) — mixes three mechanisms, adds a bespoke application to maintain, and change sets are manual and support only some metadata.
Option D (an AppExchange deployment wizard) — a packaged tool run by hand rather than a pipeline, and it may not cover every metadata type.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html

question: Universal Containers has a full sandbox that will be used to analyze and fix bugs found in production. Which two items should the architect recommend to ensure that bugs found in production are more easily analyzed in this full sandbox? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Refresh the full sandbox after every deployment in production.
optionB: Create a daily process of copying new and changed data in production to the full sandbox.
optionC: Before any deployment in production, the same process must be performed in this sandbox first.
optionD: Perform a Refresh Data in the full sandbox.
explanation:
Creating a daily process to copy new and changed production data into the full sandbox, and running every production deployment through that sandbox first, are the two recommendations. A Full sandbox can be refreshed only once every 29 days, so aligning it with production after every deployment is not something the platform allows — which forces the two that work. Copying new and changed records daily keeps the data current between refreshes, so a bug reported this morning can be reproduced against records that resemble this morning's. Running every deployment through the sandbox first keeps its metadata in step with production, so a defect reproduced there is a defect in the code rather than an artefact of drift.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (refresh the full sandbox after every production deployment) — the 29-day refresh interval makes this impossible on a Full sandbox.
Option D (perform a Refresh Data in the full sandbox) — describes an action that does not exist. Salesforce documents one refresh mechanism, which "updates its metadata from the source org" and, for a clone or template-based sandbox, "updates the org's data and its metadata". You choose which data a refresh copies, not whether to refresh data on its own.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation claimed a Refresh Data action exists and is "only available for Partial Copy and Developer Pro sandboxes". There is no such action: Salesforce documents a single refresh that updates metadata, and data too for clones and template-based sandboxes.

question: Universal Containers (UC) has developed extensions of Salesforce Service Cloud using the change set development model. Recently, UC acquired a company whose development team uses the org development model. The UC CTO wants both teams to work on a single org and follow the same set of processes. Which development model should the architect recommend for the consolidated development team?
optionA: Org development model, because the acquired company's team is already using it and it is better than the change set development model.
optionB: Package development model, because it allows packages to be created and deployed using declarative tools without writing code.
optionC: Package development model, so teams can build release artifacts that can be tested and released independently from artifacts for other projects.
optionD: Change set development model, because UC is already using it, so it will face less resistance.
explanation:
The package development model, so teams can build release artefacts that are tested and released independently, is the recommendation. Two teams merging into one org need a model where each can release without waiting on the other: work is organised into versioned packages built from source, so each team ships an artefact tested and installed on its own schedule. Scratch orgs give every feature branch a reproducible environment, and continuous integration falls out of the same source-driven arrangement.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (org development model, because the acquired team already uses it) — picks a winner by habit rather than solving how two streams share one org.
Option B (package development because it allows declarative packaging without code) — misdescribes the model: it is CLI and source driven, not a point-and-click alternative.
Option D (change sets, because UC already uses them) — the same habit argument, and change sets give no versioning and no independent release path.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has developed a managed package targeted for AppExchange. The product includes Apex code to customize and create layouts. UC is in the testing phase and the package is not yet certified. During testing on the target org, the Apex code for the layouts fails. Why are the Apex classes not able to access the metadata of the target org during testing?
optionA: Apex Settings to allow access to metadata is not switched on.
optionB: UC needs to turn on Apex Settings within the custom metadata type.
optionC: The solution is flawed. UC should utilize the Tooling API from a web service call to modify the layouts.
optionD: UC needs to get the managed package certified by the Salesforce security review.
explanation:
Apex Settings not having metadata access switched on is why the classes fail. Salesforce gates Apex metadata access on package certification but provides a switch for exactly this situation — a package still in testing. The rule is stated plainly: Apex classes in a package that has not passed security review "can't access public or protected metadata unless the Deploy Metadata from Non-Certified Package Versions via Apex org preference is enabled". That preference lives in Setup under Apex Settings and has to be turned on in the target org by an administrator, so the failure is a missing org preference in the org being tested against.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (turn on Apex Settings within the custom metadata type) — misplaces the setting: it is an org preference under Apex Settings, not something configured on a custom metadata type.
Option C (the solution is flawed, use the Tooling API) — switching API does not avoid the restriction, which is about what packaged Apex may do in a subscriber org rather than which API it calls.
Option D (get the package certified first) — certification would also lift the restriction, but waiting for security review before you can test is the wrong way round; the preference exists so uncertified packages can be exercised in a real org first.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_metadata_security.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_metadata.htm

corrected.note: Answer moved D to A. The Apex Developer Guide documents the exact control: Apex in a non-security-reviewed package cannot reach subscriber metadata unless the "Deploy Metadata from Non-Certified Package Versions via Apex" org preference is enabled, in Setup under Apex Settings. The old explanation asserted that no such Apex Settings toggle exists and that certification was the only route.

question: Universal Containers has multiple projects being developed in parallel. One project is in the testing phase and the testing team found a list of issues on items that will be deployed to production. As the project deadline is short, the customer team proposes that the fixes be done in the test sandbox and then deployed to production. What should the Architect recommend?
optionA: Recommend the customer team's proposal to fix the issues in the testing environment and deploy them to production.
optionB: Recommend fixing the issues in the development environment and deploying the changes directly to production.
optionC: Recommend fixing the issues in the development sandbox, migrating them to testing, and deploying to production after testing.
optionD: Recommend fixing the issues in the test environment and migrating the changes to the development sandbox.
explanation:
Fixing the issues in the development sandbox, migrating them to testing, and deploying to production after testing is what the architect should recommend. Changes flow one way — development, then test, then production — and a fix that enters halfway leaves the development sandbox without it; the next release from development then overwrites the fix in production and the defect returns with an authoritative-looking deployment behind it. That is the failure mode the deadline pressure is hiding.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (fix in the testing environment and deploy from there) — the customer's proposal, and exactly the regression trap above.
Option B (fix in development and deploy straight to production) — skips the verification step that produced the list of issues in the first place.
Option D (fix in test, then migrate back to development) — reverses the flow and depends on someone remembering to back-port.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management

question: Universal Containers has just initiated a project to implement a partner community. The application will be deployed into a production environment currently in use by a large Salesforce user base. The project manager has insisted that the development and testing team use a single developer sandbox. What is the risk with this approach?
optionA: Testers will encounter platform limits due to developer sandbox capacity limits.
optionB: Testers will experience functional changes throughout testing due to not having isolation from development.
optionC: Testers will hit governor limits due to large volume of users in the developer sandbox.
optionD: Refreshing the developer sandbox will take significant time.
explanation:
Testers experiencing functional changes throughout testing, because there is no isolation from development, is the risk. When developers and testers share a single sandbox, developers keep committing changes while testers are executing test cases, so the application's behaviour changes mid-cycle underneath the tests and testers observe results unrelated to real defects.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (platform limits from developer sandbox capacity) — a Developer sandbox's 200 MB data cap is a real limit, but it is not what sharing the environment causes.
Option C (governor limits from a large volume of users) — a sandbox holds no production user volume, and governor limits are per transaction rather than per environment.
Option D (refreshing will take significant time) — a Developer sandbox refreshes in minutes with a 1-day interval, and refresh time is a management concern rather than the risk of sharing.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A release will be deployed over a weekend, one week after Salesforce updates the production environment (e.g., from Winter to Spring). UC has found that a full sandbox refresh can take several days. What should the architect suggest as an optimal deployment plan?
optionA: Two weeks before go-live, deploy to Staging and then refresh the Staging and Production support sandboxes. Deploy from Staging to Production at go-live.
optionB: Approximately six weeks before go-live, ensure the sandbox will be on the release preview. One week before go-live, deploy to Staging. Deploy from Staging to Production at go-live.
optionC: One month before go-live, deploy to Staging and to Production Support. Deploy from Production Support to Production at go-live.
optionD: One week before go-live, initiate the Staging sandbox refresh and then immediately deploy to Staging. Deploy from Staging to Production at go-live.
explanation:
Ensuring the sandbox will be on the release preview about six weeks before go-live, deploying to Staging one week out, then deploying from Staging to Production at go-live is the optimal plan. Production takes the new release a week before go-live, so Staging has to be on that release when the final rehearsal runs — otherwise the deployment is proven against a platform version production is no longer on. The lever is the preview window, which sits roughly a month or more ahead of the earliest production upgrade: a sandbox created or refreshed inside it is placed on a preview instance and receives the release early.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (deploy to Staging two weeks out, then refresh Staging and Production Support) — refreshing after deploying discards the deployment, and a refresh two weeks out risks falling outside the preview window and landing on the old release, after which the 29-day interval blocks a second attempt.
Option C (deploy to Staging and Production Support a month out, ship from Production Support) — rehearses a month before the platform changes underneath it, so the tested state is not the state production will be in.
Option D (start the Staging refresh a week out and deploy immediately) — a Full sandbox refresh can run for days with no guarantee of finishing inside the window.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000380490&language=en_US&type=1
